    > - a [list](#term-series) is a rule whose two sides are each one clause
    > - the list is not a rule whose first side begins with a time phrase
    > - the list is not a rule whose second side begins with a time phrase
    >
    > then [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list without "then".
  - [`@spec a-rule-whose-first-side-begins-with-a-time-phrase-puts-its-then-on-a-line-of-its-own`](#spec-a-rule-whose-first-side-begins-with-a-time-phrase-puts-its-then-on-a-line-of-its-own) — When a [list](#term-series) is a rule whose first side begins with a time phrase, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list with "then" at the start of the second side, on a line of its own.
  - [`@spec a-rule-with-a-list-for-a-side-puts-its-then-on-a-line-of-its-own`](#spec-a-rule-with-a-list-for-a-side-puts-its-then-on-a-line-of-its-own) — When a [list](#term-series) is a rule with a first side and a second and is not a rule whose two sides are each one clause, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list with "then" at the start of the second side, on a line of its own.
  - [`@spec a-rule-that-is-a-side-of-a-rule-is-set-apart`](#spec-a-rule-that-is-a-side-of-a-rule-is-set-apart) — The verbalizer sets a rule that is a side of another rule apart, below "the following holds".
  - [`@spec a-first-side-that-holds-a-time-phrase-is-set-apart`](#spec-a-first-side-that-holds-a-time-phrase-is-set-apart) — The verbalizer sets the first side of a rule apart, below "when the following holds", when the side holds a time phrase.
  - [`@spec a-side-that-holds-a-comma-is-set-apart-where-no-then-marks-the-second-side`](#spec-a-side-that-holds-a-comma-is-set-apart-where-no-then-marks-the-second-side) — When a rule would stand on one line with no "then", the verbalizer sets apart a side with a comma of its own. When both sides hold one, it sets the second side apart.
  - [`@spec a-condition-that-is-a-series-is-said-as-a-list`](#spec-a-condition-that-is-a-series-is-said-as-a-list) — The verbalizer sets apart a condition that is a series of clauses, "a, b and c", as a list with one clause to a line.
  - [`@spec a-comma-of-a-reading-after-then-is-left-on-its-line`](#spec-a-comma-of-a-reading-after-then-is-left-on-its-line) — The verbalizer leaves on its line a second side whose only comma is inside the words of a reading, such as ", such as …" or ", with …".
  - [`@spec a-second-side-that-holds-a-time-phrase-before-an-otherwise-is-set-apart`](#spec-a-second-side-that-holds-a-time-phrase-before-an-otherwise-is-set-apart) — In a rule with an "otherwise", the verbalizer sets the second side apart when it holds a time phrase, the one it begins with included.
  - [`@spec a-second-or-last-side-of-a-rule-that-holds-a-series-is-set-apart`](#spec-a-second-or-last-side-of-a-rule-that-holds-a-series-is-set-apart) — The verbalizer sets apart a side of a rule after "then" or "otherwise" when that side is a series of clauses after a comma.
- [`@axiom a-short-list-of-rules-settles-what-english-leaves-open`](#axiom-a-short-list-of-rules-settles-what-english-leaves-open) — A short list of rules settles what English leaves open, so that each statement means only what its formula means.
  - [`@spec a-noun-phrase-covers-the-clause-it-stands-in`](#spec-a-noun-phrase-covers-the-clause-it-stands-in) — A noun phrase says its quantifier over the clause it stands in, and over nothing beyond it. "The cleanup is on no owner" says that no owner has the cleanup on it.
  - [`@spec the-first-noun-phrase-of-a-clause-covers-the-next`](#spec-the-first-noun-phrase-of-a-clause-covers-the-next) — Of two noun phrases in one clause, the first covers the second. "No cleanup is on an owner" says that no cleanup is on any owner.
  - [`@spec a-relative-clause-says-more-of-the-noun-it-follows`](#spec-a-relative-clause-says-more-of-the-noun-it-follows) — A relative clause, "that …", says what else holds of the noun right before it. An "and" inside it joins only its own conditions.
  - [`@spec the-noun-alone-names-the-one-thing-of-its-kind`](#spec-the-noun-alone-names-the-one-thing-of-its-kind) — "The cleanup" names the one cleanup the statement speaks of. Where two things of one kind are in play, each keeps its number, as "cleanup_1" and "cleanup_2" do.
  - [`@spec now-is-the-moment-a-statement-is-read-at`](#spec-now-is-the-moment-a-statement-is-read-at) — "Now" is the moment a reader takes the statement at. Inside "from now on" or "at the next moment", it is each moment that phrase picks.
  - [`@spec a-time-phrase-covers-the-rest-of-its-sentence`](#spec-a-time-phrase-covers-the-rest-of-its-sentence) — A time phrase covers the words after it up to the end of its sentence. Where it ends in a colon, it covers the lines set apart below it.
  - [`@spec until-then-stops-before-its-moment`](#spec-until-then-stops-before-its-moment) — "b now or later, and until then, a" says that b holds at some moment from now on. It says that a holds at every moment from now up to that one, and maybe not at it.
  - [`@spec the-bullets-below-a-colon-are-the-parts-of-its-line`](#spec-the-bullets-below-a-colon-are-the-parts-of-its-line) — The bullets below a line that ends in a colon are the parts of what that line says. Their indentation shows which line they belong to.
  - [`@spec a-sentence-joins-its-clauses-with-and-or-with-or-never-both`](#spec-a-sentence-joins-its-clauses-with-and-or-with-or-never-both) — A sentence joins its clauses with "and" or with "or", and never with both. A list shows how such clauses group.
  - [`@spec exactly-when-goes-both-ways-and-when-goes-one`](#spec-exactly-when-goes-both-ways-and-when-goes-one) — "x exactly when y" says that each holds where the other does. "When x, y" says that y holds wherever x does, and nothing of the moments without x.
  - [`@spec another-differs-from-the-thing-of-its-kind-named-last`](#spec-another-differs-from-the-thing-of-its-kind-named-last) — "Another unit" and "no other unit" differ from the unit the words named last before them. That unit is in the same clause, in the clause before it, or where a quantifier introduced it.
  - [`@spec one-of-these-names-one-of-kinds-that-share-no-member`](#spec-one-of-these-names-one-of-kinds-that-share-no-member) — "x is one of these:" says that x is what one of the phrases below it names. The phrases name kinds that share no member, so x is never two of them.
  - [`@spec a-noun-the-words-name-again-in-a-when-is-every-thing-of-its-kind`](#spec-a-noun-the-words-name-again-in-a-when-is-every-thing-of-its-kind) — "A bug" stands for every bug where "the bug" follows it, in the first side of a rule or as the subject of "exactly when". "When a bug has run, code has registered the bug" says that of each bug.
  - [`@spec each-statement-reads-back-to-its-meaning`](#spec-each-statement-reads-back-to-its-meaning) — Read by these rules, the words of each statement have one meaning, and it is the meaning of what the verbalizer said.
  - [`@spec each-fixed-word-of-the-printer-reads-back-to-its-meaning`](#spec-each-fixed-word-of-the-printer-reads-back-to-its-meaning) — Each fixed word of the printer stands in a statement that reads back to its one meaning. These are the intros of its lists, its time phrases, the parts of `until` and `since`, and the words of rules and of comparisons.
<!-- toc:end -->

## Terms

### @term verbalizer

> The verbalizer is the part of naturalloy that says a formula in words, from a table of readings that says each name of the formula.

A reading gives the positive and the negative words for a set, a field, a relation or a predicate. A noun gives the words for a signature.

```alloy bounds
for 6
```

### @term formula

> A formula is a piece of Alloy that states a claim, and that the verbalizer says in words.

### @term quantified-formula

> A quantified formula is a formula that declares variables, and the verbalizer names them and says their types.

### @term quantifier

> A quantifier is a formula that declares a variable and says something of it, which the verbalizer may say as a noun phrase.

```alloy vocabulary
sig Quantifier {}
sig VariableOnce, AsNounPhrase, VariableSubject, AsSubjectPhrase, VariableWithCondition, RelativeClause in Quantifier {}
sig OneNegation, SaysAnother, NestsPhrases in Quantifier {}
sig VariableTwice, NothingToAttach, NoWithAnother, ConditionAside, TimedCondition, InFull in Quantifier {}
sig ThereIsThat, ThereIsThatList, LongConditions, NoUnderNo, UnderNo in Quantifier {}
fact quantifier_wordings { no AsNounPhrase & InFull and no ThereIsThat & InFull and no ThereIsThatList & InFull and no ThereIsThat & ThereIsThatList and AsSubjectPhrase + RelativeClause + OneNegation + SaysAnother + NestsPhrases in AsNounPhrase and no VariableOnce & VariableTwice }
```

```readings
noun Quantifier: [quantifier]
VariableOnce: the sentence says the variable of {1} once | the sentence does not say the variable of {1} once
AsNounPhrase: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as a noun phrase in the place of the variable, such as "sits in no unit" | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as a noun phrase in the place of the variable, such as "sits in no unit"
VariableSubject: the variable of {1} is the subject of the sentence | the variable of {1} is not the subject of the sentence
AsSubjectPhrase: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} with the noun phrase as the subject, such as "a tag names unit_1" | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} with the noun phrase as the subject, such as "a tag names unit_1"
VariableWithCondition: the variable of {1} has a further condition | the variable of {1} has no further condition
RelativeClause: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} with a relative clause, such as "a unit that is a spec" | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} with a relative clause, such as "a unit that is a spec"
OneNegation: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} with one negation that lists the kinds | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} with one negation that lists the kinds
SaysAnother: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} with "another" before the noun | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} with "another" before the noun
NestsPhrases: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as nested phrases, such as "a test checks a bug that sits in unit_1" | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as nested phrases, such as "a test checks a bug that sits in unit_1"
VariableTwice: the reading of {1} says the variable twice | the reading of {1} does not say the variable twice
NothingToAttach: {1} has no fact for its variable beside another thing | {1} has a fact for its variable beside another thing
NoWithAnother: {1} says no variable differs from another and holds a condition | {1} does not both say that no variable differs from another and hold a condition
ConditionAside: the condition of {1} is not about its variable | the condition of {1} is about its variable
TimedCondition: {1} has several conditions, one of which begins with a time phrase | {1} does not have several conditions, one of which begins with a time phrase
InFull: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} in full, with "there is" and the numbered name | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} in full, with "there is" and the numbered name
ThereIsThat: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as "there is" with its noun and a relative clause, such as "there is a unit that is a spec", or under "no" with one condition, such as "no unit is a spec" | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as "there is" with its noun and a relative clause, such as "there is a unit that is a spec", or under "no" with one condition, such as "no unit is a spec"
ThereIsThatList: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as "there is" with its noun and "that", and its conditions as bullets below it without their subject | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as "there is" with its noun and "that", and its conditions as bullets below it without their subject
UnderNo: {1} is under "no" | {1} is not under "no"
LongConditions: {1} has more than three conditions, or conditions longer than a line | {1} has three conditions or fewer that fit a line
NoUnderNo: {1} is under "no" with a condition that says "no" | {1} is not under "no" with a condition that says "no"
```

> - the sentence says the variable of the quantifier once
> - the quantifier says no variable differs from another and holds a condition

```alloy scenario
some f: Quantifier | f in VariableOnce and f in NoWithAnother
```

> - the reading of the quantifier says the variable twice

> - the condition of the quantifier is not about its variable
<!-- statement-scenario-3-term-quantifier:end -->

```alloy scenario
some f: Quantifier | f in VariableOnce and f in ConditionAside
```

> There is a quantifier such that all of these hold:

> - the quantifier has no fact for its variable beside another thing

```alloy scenario
some f: Quantifier | f in VariableWithCondition and f in NothingToAttach
```

### @term fit

<!-- statement-term-fit:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> A [quantifier](#term-quantifier) fits a noun phrase exactly when all of these hold:
> - the reading of the quantifier does not say the variable twice
> - the quantifier has a fact for its variable beside another thing
> - the quantifier does not both say that no variable differs from another and hold a condition
> - the condition of the quantifier is about its variable
> - the quantifier does not have several conditions, one of which begins with a time phrase
<!-- statement-term-fit:end -->

A quantifier fits a noun phrase, such as "sits in no unit", unless that short form would mislead. A noun phrase stands for one thing in one place, so the reading must say the variable only once. The phrase also needs another thing in the sentence to hang from, and its condition must be about the variable itself. "No" with "another" rules it out, since "no other" hints at what the logic does not say. So does a time phrase that leads one of several conditions, since it seems to cover them all.

```alloy
pred fits[f: Quantifier] { f not in VariableTwice and f not in NothingToAttach and f not in NoWithAnother and f not in ConditionAside and f not in TimedCondition }
```

```readings
fits: {1} [fits] a noun phrase | {1} does not [fit] a noun phrase
```

### @term predicate-call

> A predicate call is a formula that names a predicate and gives its arguments.

### @term definition-passage

> A definition is a predicate with a body that the verbalizer says as what its name means exactly when the body holds.

```alloy vocabulary
sig Definition {}
sig GuardedByKind, PhrasePerKind, SameKindTwice, JoinedWithOr, OrInsideKind, OneCoordination in Definition {}
sig OneKind, OneSentenceKind, NoKindFirst, AmbiguousAnd, NotAboutSubject, KindsShareAMember, AsItStands in Definition {}
fact case_wordings { no PhrasePerKind & AsItStands and JoinedWithOr + OneCoordination + OneSentenceKind in PhrasePerKind and no GuardedByKind & NoKindFirst }
```

```readings
noun Definition: [definition]
GuardedByKind: the alternatives of {1} each begin with the kind of the subject | the alternatives of {1} do not each begin with the kind of the subject
PhrasePerKind: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as a list with a noun phrase for each kind, such as "a spec that cites no axiom" | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as a list with a noun phrase for each kind, such as "a spec that cites no axiom"
SameKindTwice: {1} has two alternatives for one kind | {1} does not have two alternatives for one kind
JoinedWithOr: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as one noun phrase for that kind, with the alternatives joined by or | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as one noun phrase for that kind, with the alternatives joined by or
OrInsideKind: {1} has an or inside one kind | {1} has no or inside one kind
OneCoordination: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as one run of clauses joined by commas and or | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as one run of clauses joined by commas and or
OneKind: the alternatives of {1} are of one kind | the alternatives of {1} are not of one kind
OneSentenceKind: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as one sentence | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as one sentence
NoKindFirst: {1} has an alternative that does not begin with its kind | {1} has no alternative that does not begin with its kind
AmbiguousAnd: {1} has a run of "and" beside another alternative of its kind | {1} has no run of "and" beside another alternative of its kind
NotAboutSubject: {1} has an alternative that says something about another unit | {1} has no alternative that says something about another unit
KindsShareAMember: {1} has two kinds that can share a member | {1} does not have two kinds that can share a member
AsItStands: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as a list of the alternatives as they stand | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as a list of the alternatives as they stand
```

> - has a run of "and" beside another alternative of its kind
<!-- statement-scenario-1-term-definition-passage:end -->


> There is a definition such that all of these hold:

<!-- statement-scenario-2-term-definition-passage:end -->


> There is a definition that has an or inside one kind and has an alternative that does not begin with its kind.
<!-- statement-scenario-3-term-definition-passage:end -->

### @term by-kind

<!-- statement-term-by-kind:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> A [definition](#term-definition-passage) can be said kind by kind exactly when the definition has none of these:
> - an alternative that does not begin with its kind
> - a run of "and" beside another alternative of its kind
> - an alternative that says something about another unit
> - two kinds that can share a member
<!-- statement-term-by-kind:end -->

The verbalizer can say a definition kind by kind when each alternative turns cleanly into a phrase for its kind. Every alternative must open with its kind, because the phrase starts with the kind. Every alternative must be about the subject, because the phrase describes the subject. No run of "and" may stand beside another alternative of the same kind, where a reader could not tell which one it joins. And no two of its kinds may share a member, because a reader can take "one of these" as exactly one.

```alloy
pred byKind[d: Definition] { d not in NoKindFirst and d not in AmbiguousAnd and d not in NotAboutSubject and d not in KindsShareAMember }
```

```readings
byKind: {1} can be said [kind by kind] | {1} cannot be said [kind by kind]
```

### @term linked-formula

> A linked formula is a formula that has a word whose reading a unit holds, and the statement may link that word.

### @term series

> A series is a run of clauses, or a rule of two sides. The verbalizer says it as a sentence, as bullets or on one line.

A list becomes a sentence only if six things hold:

- It has three clauses or fewer.
- Every item is one clause.
- No item holds a comma, unless the list has two clauses.
- The sentence fits a line.
- No clause before the last begins with a time phrase.
- No clause before the last holds a relative clause.

Any other list becomes bullets.

```alloy vocabulary
sig Series {}
sig Items, Rule, Few, Many, MoreThanTwo, NotClause, CommaItem, TooLong, AndInOr, TimeBeforeLast, RelativeBeforeLast in Series {}
sig AsSentence, AsBullets, KeepsAndApart, SharedSubject, PairInList, SharedNegatives, SaysNoneOfThese in Series {}
sig OneLineRule, TimeFirst, TimeSecond, OneLine, KeepsThen, DropsThen, ThenOwnLine in Series {}
fact series_wordings { no Items & Rule and Items = Few + Many and no Few & Many and Many in MoreThanTwo and AndInOr in NotClause and no AsSentence & AsBullets and KeepsAndApart in AsBullets and (Few + Many + NotClause + CommaItem + TooLong + TimeBeforeLast + RelativeBeforeLast + SharedSubject + PairInList) in Items and (OneLineRule + TimeFirst + TimeSecond) in Rule and no KeepsThen & DropsThen and no OneLine & ThenOwnLine and (KeepsThen + DropsThen) in OneLine and ThenOwnLine in Rule and SharedNegatives in Items and SaysNoneOfThese in AsBullets }
```

```readings
noun Series: [list]
Items: {1} is a run of clauses joined by and or by or | {1} is not a run of clauses joined by and or by or
Rule: {1} is a rule with a first side and a second | {1} is not a rule with a first side and a second
Few: {1} has three clauses or fewer | {1} does not have three clauses or fewer
Many: {1} has more than three clauses | {1} does not have more than three clauses
MoreThanTwo: {1} has more than two clauses | {1} has two clauses or fewer
NotClause: {1} has an item that is more than one clause | {1} has only items that are one clause
CommaItem: {1} has an item that holds a comma | {1} has no item that holds a comma
TooLong: {1} is longer than a line when it is put in a sentence | {1} fits a line when it is put in a sentence
TimeBeforeLast: {1} has a clause before its last that begins with a time phrase | {1} has no clause before its last that begins with a time phrase
RelativeBeforeLast: {1} has a clause before its last with a relative clause in it | {1} has no clause before its last with a relative clause in it
AndInOr: {1} is a list of alternatives where one alternative holds an and | {1} is not a list of alternatives where one alternative holds an and
AsSentence: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} in a sentence | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} in a sentence
AsBullets: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as bullets | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as bullets
KeepsAndApart: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} as bullets that cannot be read two ways | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} as bullets that cannot be read two ways
SharedSubject: {1} has clauses that begin with the same subject | {1} has no clauses that begin with the same subject
PairInList: {1} has a clause about a pair of variables | {1} has no clause about a pair of variables
SharedNegatives: {1} is a run of negative clauses about one subject that share their verb, each before a noun phrase of its own | {1} is not a run of negative clauses about one subject that share their verb, each before a noun phrase of its own
SaysNoneOfThese: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the subject and the verb that the clauses of {1} share once, before "none of these" | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say the subject and the verb that the clauses of {1} share once, before "none of these"
OneLineRule: {1} is a rule whose two sides are each one clause | {1} is not a rule whose two sides are each one clause
TimeFirst: {1} is a rule whose first side begins with a time phrase | {1} is not a rule whose first side begins with a time phrase
TimeSecond: {1} is a rule whose second side begins with a time phrase | {1} is not a rule whose second side begins with a time phrase
OneLine: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} on one line, as "when" the first side, the second side | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} on one line, as "when" the first side, the second side
KeepsThen: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} with "then" before the time phrase | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} with "then" before the time phrase
DropsThen: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} without "then" | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} without "then"
ThenOwnLine: [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says {1} with "then" at the start of the second side, on a line of its own | [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) does not say {1} with "then" at the start of the second side, on a line of its own
```

### @term sentenceable

<!-- statement-term-sentenceable:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> A [list](#term-series) can be put in a sentence exactly when all of these hold:
> - the list has three clauses or fewer
> - the list has only items that are one clause
> - at least one of these holds:
>   - the list has no item that holds a comma
>   - the list has two clauses or fewer
> - the list fits a line when it is put in a sentence
> - the list has no clause before its last that begins with a time phrase
> - the list has no clause before its last with a relative clause in it
<!-- statement-term-sentenceable:end -->

A list goes in a sentence only when a reader can take it in at once. That means at most three items, each a single clause, and the whole on one line. A comma inside an item is fine in a pair, but in a list of three it blurs where the items end. A time phrase or a relative clause before the last clause would seem to cover the rest, so it keeps the list out too.

```alloy
pred sentenceable[f: Series] { f in Few and f not in NotClause and (f not in CommaItem or f not in MoreThanTwo) and f not in TooLong and f not in TimeBeforeLast and f not in RelativeBeforeLast }
```

```readings
sentenceable: {1} can be put in a [sentence] | {1} cannot be put in a [sentence]
```

### @term line

> A line is one line of a table of readings, which gives a word of the logic its sentences.

### @term pass

> A pass is one named change to how the verbalizer says a statement. A pass of the IR changes the sentence a formula was lowered to. A pass of the printer changes the words the printer lays it out in.

```alloy vocabulary
sig Pass { ahead: set Pass }
sig OfIR, OfPrinter in Pass {}
sig NegationInward, AnotherOfAKind, NounPhrases, ThereIsAThat, XAndNoOther, ForEveryTogether, UntilInASentence, TimePhraseInFront, ClausesInASentence, NoneOfThese, RuleOnOneLine in Pass {}
fact passes {
  Pass = OfIR + OfPrinter and no OfIR & OfPrinter
  NegationInward + AnotherOfAKind + NounPhrases + ThereIsAThat + XAndNoOther + ForEveryTogether + UntilInASentence + TimePhraseInFront + ClausesInASentence + NoneOfThese + RuleOnOneLine in OfIR
}
```

```readings
noun Pass: [pass]
ahead: {1} runs before {2} | {1} does not run before {2}
OfIR: {1} changes the IR | {1} does not change the IR
OfPrinter: {1} changes the options of the printer | {1} does not change the options of the printer
NegationInward: {1} moves a negation inward | {1} does not move a negation inward
AnotherOfAKind: {1} says two things of a kind as one and another | {1} does not say two things of a kind as one and another
NounPhrases: {1} says a quantifier as a noun phrase | {1} does not say a quantifier as a noun phrase
ThereIsAThat: {1} says a quantifier of its variable alone as "there is a … that" | {1} does not say a quantifier of its variable alone as "there is a … that"
XAndNoOther: {1} says a set equal to a variable as that variable and no other | {1} does not say a set equal to a variable as that variable and no other
ForEveryTogether: {1} makes nested quantifiers of "for every" one | {1} does not make nested quantifiers of "for every" one
UntilInASentence: {1} says until and since of two clauses as one sentence | {1} does not say until and since of two clauses as one sentence
TimePhraseInFront: {1} puts a time phrase in front of the words it covers | {1} does not put a time phrase in front of the words it covers
ClausesInASentence: {1} says a few clauses as one sentence | {1} does not say a few clauses as one sentence
NoneOfThese: {1} says the subject and the verb that negative clauses share once, before "none of these" | {1} does not say the subject and the verb that negative clauses share once, before "none of these"
RuleOnOneLine: {1} says a rule on one line | {1} does not say a rule on one line
```

### @term pipeline

> The pipeline is the passes in the order they run: each sees the IR the one before it left.

## @fact every-moment-has-a-next-moment

> In Alloy 6, a trace is infinite: every moment has exactly one next moment.

The analyzer checks temporal formulas over traces that loop back, so `after f` is never true for want of a next moment. The [Alloy 6 documentation](https://alloytools.org/alloy6.html) says so.

## @fact the-analyzer-wraps-integers-at-their-bit-width

> With its default options, the analyzer keeps every integer in a fixed bit width. A number that leaves that range wraps around into it.

Checked with the analyzer of Alloy 6.2.0, with the default of 4 bits, which holds the integers from -8 to 7:

- `plus[7, 1]` is -8.
- `9 = -7` holds.
- A count of 9 things is -7.

`A4Options.noOverflow` is false unless a run sets it, and the canon plugin runs the analyzer with its defaults.

## @fact the-analyzer-divides-toward-zero-and-gives-the-sign-for-zero

> The analyzer rounds `div[a, b]` toward zero, and gives -1, 0 or 1 for `div[a, 0]` as `a` is positive, zero or negative. `rem[a, b]` has the sign of `a`, and `rem[a, 0]` is `a`.

Checked with the analyzer of Alloy 6.2.0: `div[-7, 2] = -3`, `div[5, 0] = -1`, `div[-5, 0] = 1`, `div[0, 0] = 0`, `rem[-7, 2] = -1`.

## @fact the-analyzer-shifts-by-the-lowest-bits-of-the-amount

> The analyzer shifts by the number in the lowest bits of the amount: as many bits as it takes to count to the bit width.

With 5 bits, `1 << 9` is `1 << 1`, and `1 << 7` and `1 << -1` are 0. Checked with the analyzer of Alloy 6.2.0.

## @axiom a-formula-is-said-without-loss

> The verbalizer says a formula only in words that translate it without loss, and refuses a formula that it cannot say that way.

This follows because a reader learns from the words what the formula claims. Words that say more or less than the formula mislead that reader, so a refusal is better than a loss. How natural the words sound comes after.

#### @spec a-statement-is-said-through-passes-that-each-keep-its-meaning

> The verbalizer lowers a formula to the IR in the plainest words its readings give. It makes each choice of words in a [pass](#term-pass) of the [pipeline](#term-pipeline). A pass of the IR changes no meaning. The analyzer asks that of every change it makes to the sweep.

This follows because a choice of words made in one place can be checked in one place. The literal reading is lossless by construction, and each pass after it keeps what the reading means. So the words keep it too.

##### @spec every-pass-changes-the-words-of-a-formula-of-the-sweep

> Every [pass](#term-pass) changes the words of at least one formula of the sweep.

This follows because the sweep is where a pass is checked. The analyzer asks whether each change to the IR of the sweep keeps its meaning, and the parser reads the words back. A pass that changes no formula of the sweep is checked by neither, only by the examples of its own tests. For a pass that only chooses a layout, which changes no meaning, the reading back is the whole check. Until the sweep gained formulas for them, three passes changed none of its words.

##### @spec a-pass-runs-after-the-passes-whose-shapes-it-reads

> Where one pass makes or removes a shape that another reads, the [pipeline](#term-pipeline) runs them in the order the shape needs.

This follows because a pass sees only the IR the passes before it left. Run in the other order, a pass would miss the shape it changes, or change a shape another pass needed first.

###### @spec a-negation-moves-inward-before-noun-phrases-are-said

<!-- statement-spec-a-negation-moves-inward-before-noun-phrases-are-said:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> For every [pass_1](#term-pass) and every pass_2:
>
> when pass_1 moves a negation inward and pass_2 says a quantifier as a noun phrase, pass_1 runs before pass_2.
<!-- statement-spec-a-negation-moves-inward-before-noun-phrases-are-said:end -->

A noun phrase with "no" comes from a quantifier "no". A negated quantifier "some" becomes one only once its negation moves inward. So a reader gets "no cleanup has run", and not a negation set apart above the quantifier.

```alloy
all a: NegationInward, b: NounPhrases | a->b in ahead
```

###### @spec two-things-of-a-kind-are-paired-before-noun-phrases-are-said

<!-- statement-spec-two-things-of-a-kind-are-paired-before-noun-phrases-are-said:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> For every [pass_1](#term-pass) and every pass_2:
>
> when pass_1 says two things of a kind as one and another and pass_2 says a quantifier as a noun phrase, pass_1 runs before pass_2.
<!-- statement-spec-two-things-of-a-kind-are-paired-before-noun-phrases-are-said:end -->

"A unit and another unit" says two things of one kind that differ, each with what holds of it. Said first as noun phrases one inside the other, they would lose the pair. The difference between them would stay a clause of its own.

```alloy
all a: AnotherOfAKind, b: NounPhrases | a->b in ahead
```

###### @spec noun-phrases-are-said-before-there-is-a-that

<!-- statement-spec-noun-phrases-are-said-before-there-is-a-that:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> For every [pass_1](#term-pass) and every pass_2:
>
> when all of these hold:
> - pass_1 says a quantifier as a noun phrase
> - pass_2 says a quantifier of its variable alone as "there is a … that"
>
> then pass_1 runs before pass_2.
<!-- statement-spec-noun-phrases-are-said-before-there-is-a-that:end -->

A noun phrase hangs the variable from something the sentence already names, and reads better than a sentence of its own. The form with "that" is for a variable with nothing to hang from, so it takes what the noun phrases leave.

```alloy
all a: NounPhrases, b: ThereIsAThat | a->b in ahead
```

###### @spec a-set-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-before-quantifiers-of-for-every-become-one

<!-- statement-spec-a-set-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-before-quantifiers-of-for-every-become-one:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> For every [pass_1](#term-pass) and every pass_2:
>
> when all of these hold:
> - pass_1 says a set equal to a variable as that variable and no other
> - pass_2 makes nested quantifiers of "for every" one
>
> then pass_1 runs before pass_2.
<!-- statement-spec-a-set-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-before-quantifiers-of-for-every-become-one:end -->

"The cleanup is on owner_1 and is on no other owner" comes from a "for every" over the members of the set. It sits right inside the "for every" that names the cleanup, and once the two become one, the pass cannot find it.

```alloy
all a: XAndNoOther, b: ForEveryTogether | a->b in ahead
```

###### @spec until-is-said-in-a-sentence-before-a-time-phrase-goes-in-front

<!-- statement-spec-until-is-said-in-a-sentence-before-a-time-phrase-goes-in-front:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> For every [pass_1](#term-pass) and every pass_2:
>
> when all of these hold:
> - pass_1 says until and since of two clauses as one sentence
> - pass_2 puts a time phrase in front of the words it covers
>
> then pass_1 runs before pass_2.
<!-- statement-spec-until-is-said-in-a-sentence-before-a-time-phrase-goes-in-front:end -->

"b now or later, and until then, a" holds a time phrase of its own. A time phrase in front of it would read as one moment with it. So the pass that puts one there must see the sentence the `until` became.

```alloy
all a: UntilInASentence, b: TimePhraseInFront | a->b in ahead
```

###### @spec a-time-phrase-goes-in-front-before-clauses-become-a-sentence

<!-- statement-spec-a-time-phrase-goes-in-front-before-clauses-become-a-sentence:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> For every [pass_1](#term-pass) and every pass_2:
>
> when pass_1 puts a time phrase in front of the words it covers and pass_2 says a few clauses as one sentence, pass_1 runs before pass_2.
<!-- statement-spec-a-time-phrase-goes-in-front-before-clauses-become-a-sentence:end -->

"c has run and at the next moment, pulse has disposed o" puts a clause at the next moment beside another. That clause is one line only once its time phrase stands in front of it, so the clauses can become one sentence only after.

```alloy
all a: TimePhraseInFront, b: ClausesInASentence | a->b in ahead
```

###### @spec clauses-become-a-sentence-before-a-rule-goes-on-one-line

<!-- statement-spec-clauses-become-a-sentence-before-a-rule-goes-on-one-line:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> For every [pass_1](#term-pass) and every pass_2:
>
> when pass_1 says a few clauses as one sentence and pass_2 says a rule on one line, pass_1 runs before pass_2.
<!-- statement-spec-clauses-become-a-sentence-before-a-rule-goes-on-one-line:end -->

A rule goes on one line only when each side is one line. A side of several clauses is one line only once those clauses are a sentence.

```alloy
all a: ClausesInASentence, b: RuleOnOneLine | a->b in ahead
```

###### @spec clauses-become-a-sentence-before-their-shared-words-are-said-once

<!-- statement-spec-clauses-become-a-sentence-before-their-shared-words-are-said-once:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> For every [pass_1](#term-pass) and every pass_2:
>
> when all of these hold:
> - pass_1 says a few clauses as one sentence
> - pass_2 says the subject and the verb that negative clauses share once, before "none of these"
>
> then pass_1 runs before pass_2.
<!-- statement-spec-clauses-become-a-sentence-before-their-shared-words-are-said-once:end -->

A list of a few clauses reads best as a sentence, and "none of these" only shortens the bullets of a list that stays bullets. So the clauses that can become a sentence do so first, and only the lists left as bullets say their shared words once.

```alloy
all a: ClausesInASentence, b: NoneOfThese | a->b in ahead
```

##### @spec a-pass-weighs-only-words-that-no-later-pass-changes

> The words a [pass](#term-pass) weighs to choose how to say a part are the words that part ends with: no pass after it changes them.

This follows because a pass that weighs words decides from them, as a layout decides from them whether a part fits on a line. If a later pass changes those words, the choice rests on words the reader never sees, and it is right only by luck. Each order spec above names one such dependence. This spec says what they all serve, so that a test can find a dependence no spec names. Over the sweep, the test takes each part a pass weighed and left as it was, and asks whether a later pass changed it.

###### @bug a-time-phrase-weighs-a-part-that-a-later-pass-changes

> The verbalizer weighs whether a time phrase goes in front before it lays out the rule or the list the phrase covers. So a time phrase can stay above a rule that ends on one line.

Over the sweep this happens in 15 formulas. In 12 of them a rule ends on one line below "from now on:", where the time phrase could stand in front. The words lose nothing, but they are not the words the layout specs choose. No order of the three passes fixes it: the time phrase weighs what the other two make, and they must run after it. Settling the layout of each part before the part that holds it weighs it would.

Issue: #76

#### @spec a-formula-is-said-in-full

> The verbalizer says every part of a [formula](#term-formula), and leaves none unsaid.

This follows because a statement that leaves a part of its formula out says less than the logic holds.

#### @spec a-formula-is-said-the-same-way-every-time

> The verbalizer says a formula in the same words every time.

This follows because a reader who sees the statement change between two runs cannot tell whether the logic changed.

#### @spec saying-a-formula-ends

> The verbalizer ends on every formula, with words or with a refusal.

This follows because a formula the verbalizer never finishes is neither said nor refused. The reader learns neither its words nor why it has none. A rewrite that comes back to a formula the verbalizer is still saying would never end, so it is a fault of the verbalizer.

#### @spec a-refusal-is-told-apart-from-a-fault

> The verbalizer refuses a formula only with a `Refusal`, and anything else it throws is a fault of the verbalizer.

This follows because a refusal tells the author what to change in the formula or its readings. A fault that looked like one would send the author to mend a formula that has words, and would hide the fault.

#### @spec a-rewrite-means-what-the-formula-it-replaces-means

> Where the verbalizer says a formula through another, the two hold at the same moments, for every value of their free variables.

This follows because the words say the formula the verbalizer rewrote to, and not the one the author wrote. A rewrite that changed the meaning would change the claim, even where the words say the rewrite well. The analyzer can look for a world where the two differ, so this claim is checked and not only read.

#### @spec a-quantifier-is-said-with-the-noun-of-its-type-for-each-variable

> The verbalizer says each variable of a [quantified formula](#term-quantified-formula) once, with the noun of its type.

This follows because the noun tells the reader what kind of thing the variable stands for, and each variable is a thing of its own.

#### @spec three-things-a-for-every-names-are-a-list

> When "for every" or "for some" names three things or more, the verbalizer lists them: "for every cleanup, every owner_1 and every owner_2".

This follows because English lists three things with commas and one "and". A run of "and … and …" reads as speech, and makes the reader count.

#### @spec some-of-several-things-is-said-as-for-some

> The verbalizer says `some` over several variables as "for some" each of them, followed by what holds of them, the way it says `all` as "for every".

This follows because the old form put a plural verb before a single noun, and "such that" is the language of logic. "For some" reads like "for every", which the reader already knows. Over one variable, the old sentence stays, since it reads as English.

#### @spec a-for-every-right-inside-a-for-every-is-one-for-every

> The verbalizer says a "for every" whose formula is another "for every" as one, with the variables of both: "for every cleanup and every owner".

This follows because for every x, for every y, a formula holds exactly when for every x and every y it holds. The second "for every" on a line of its own adds a level of indent and nothing else.

#### @spec a-variable-is-named-after-its-noun-and-its-number

> Where a variable needs a number, the verbalizer names it after its noun and its number among the variables of that noun.

This follows because a name such as unit_1 tells the reader the kind of the variable wherever it shows. The number tells it apart from the other units.

#### @spec a-variable-alone-of-its-noun-is-named-the-noun

> The verbalizer names a variable "the" and its noun, with no number, when a quantifier says it first. No other variable may have its noun, and no other word of the statement may say that noun.

This follows because "the unit" can then point at one thing only. A number that tells nothing apart is one more thing to read. A variable that a count says first keeps its number: "the values of the owner" would read as the values of one owner.

#### @spec a-for-every-over-the-noun-alone-is-said-as-a-noun-where-the-words-first-name-it

> Take a "for every" over one variable that is named the noun alone. The words may first name the variable in the first side of a rule, or as the subject of a definition. There, the verbalizer leaves the "for every" out. It says that first name as "a" or "an" and the noun, and each later one as "the" and the noun. The words must name the variable again after the first time.

Derives from: [`spec-a-variable-alone-of-its-noun-is-named-the-noun`](#spec-a-variable-alone-of-its-noun-is-named-the-noun), [`spec-a-noun-the-words-name-again-in-a-when-is-every-thing-of-its-kind`](#spec-a-noun-the-words-name-again-in-a-when-is-every-thing-of-its-kind)

This follows because the reading rules give "a bug" in a "when" the meaning of every bug. A line "for every bug:" above the rule then tells the reader nothing more. A variable named only once would leave "a bug" free to mean one bug or every bug, so the words keep the "for every" there.

```text
When a cleanup has run, code has registered the cleanup.
```

##### @spec a-rule-over-every-thing-of-a-kind-says-a-noun-in-its-when

> The verbalizer says a "for every" over one variable as the rule it holds, where that rule has no "otherwise". Its first side says "a" and the noun: "when a cleanup has run, code has registered the cleanup".

This follows because English states a rule over a kind this way, and the words keep the meaning the "for every" gave them.

##### @spec a-definition-of-every-thing-of-a-kind-says-a-noun-as-its-subject

> The verbalizer says a definition over one parameter as its words alone, where they open with the parameter. Their subject is "a" and the noun: "a unit is unfounded exactly when the unit is one of these".

This follows because a definition says what a word means of any one thing of its kind. "A unit is … exactly when …" says that the way a glossary does.

##### @spec a-variable-named-once-keeps-its-for-every

> Where the words name the variable of a "for every" only once, the verbalizer keeps the "for every".

This follows because "a bug" with no "the bug" after it could mean some bug or every bug. Only every bug is what the formula says.

##### @spec a-rule-with-an-otherwise-keeps-its-for-every

> The verbalizer keeps the "for every" of a rule that has an "otherwise".

This follows because the "otherwise" speaks of the things for which the first side does not hold. A reader who took "a bug" in the first side as some bug would read the "otherwise" as the case where no bug does.

#### @spec a-variable-is-named-the-same-however-the-formula-names-it

> The verbalizer names the variables the same way, whatever names the formula gives them.

This follows because the name the author chose says nothing about the logic, and a statement must not change when the author renames a variable.

#### @spec some-is-said-with-an-article-chosen-by-the-sound-of-the-noun

> The verbalizer says `some` of a type with the article "a" or "an" that fits the sound of the noun.

This follows because English picks the article from the sound of the noun, and a reader notices a wrong one.

#### @spec an-article-the-noun-is-written-with-wins-over-its-sound

> When the noun of a type carries an article, the verbalizer uses that article, whatever the sound of the noun.

This follows because the author knows the word better than the sound rule, and an hour is an hour.

#### @spec no-over-several-variables-is-said-as-no-combination

> The verbalizer says `no` over variables of several types as no combination of the variables.

This follows because a statement that none of each variable exists would mean something else than none of them together.

#### @spec one-as-a-quantifier-is-said-as-exactly-one

> The verbalizer says `one` over a variable as "exactly one" of its noun, and over several variables as exactly one combination of them.

This follows because `one` holds when the body holds for one value of the variables and for no other. Over several variables, the value is the combination.

#### @spec lone-as-a-quantifier-is-said-as-at-most-one

> The verbalizer says `lone` over a variable as "at most one" of its noun, and over several variables as at most one combination of them.

This follows because `lone` holds when the body holds for no value of the variables or for one.

#### @spec a-block-as-the-body-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-its-formulas-together

> The verbalizer says a quantifier whose body is a block, `all x: T { a b }`, as the quantifier with the formulas of the block holding together.

This follows because the formulas of a block hold together, as if `and` joined them.

#### @spec a-call-of-a-predicate-gives-its-variables-numbers-that-are-free

> When a called body quantifies a variable that the call already uses, the verbalizer gives it a number that no variable in use has.

This follows because a reader takes two variables with one name for one variable, and the statement would say what the logic does not.

#### @spec a-variable-of-a-body-never-takes-the-name-of-an-argument

> The verbalizer never gives a variable of a called body the name of an argument of the call.

This follows because the argument and the variable would read as one thing.

#### @spec the-alternatives-of-a-list-reuse-a-name-and-keep-it-taken-for-what-follows

> The verbalizer gives the same name to the variable in each alternative of a list, and keeps the name taken for what follows.

This follows because alternatives do not hold together, so one name in each is clear. What follows must not reuse a name an alternative took.

#### @spec the-statements-of-a-list-each-use-the-same-names

> The verbalizer uses the same names in each statement of a list that quantifies a variable of one type.

This follows because statements of a list stand apart, and a reader reads each from its own start.

#### @spec conditions-that-hold-together-keep-their-names-apart

> The verbalizer gives a different name to the variable of each condition in a list of conditions that hold together.

This follows because conditions that hold together may talk about the same thing, and one name would join what the logic keeps apart.

#### @spec a-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body

> The verbalizer says a [call](#term-predicate-call) of a predicate with no reading by its body, with each argument in the place it fills.

This follows because the author gave the predicate a body so that it means something, and the body is the next best words.

#### @spec a-negated-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-as-untrue

> The verbalizer says a negated call of a predicate with no reading as "it is not the case that", followed by the body. It sets a body that is more than one plain clause apart below those words.

This follows because the negative of a body has no words of its own, so the sentence says that the body does not hold. Before a body of two clauses on the same line, a reader could take the "not" as covering only the first.

#### @spec the-reading-of-the-table-wins-over-the-body

> The verbalizer says a call of a predicate that has both a reading and a body with the reading.

This follows because the table is where the author says how a word sounds, and the body is a fallback.

#### @spec the-checker-reads-the-predicates-a-vocabulary-declares

> The verbalizer reads each predicate that a vocabulary declares: its name, what it takes and its body.

This follows because the verbalizer can use only the body of a predicate that has no reading, and the body lives in the vocabulary.

#### @spec a-call-written-as-a-join-is-said-as-the-call

> The verbalizer says `x.p` and `x.p[y]`, for a predicate `p`, as `p[x]` and `p[x, y]`.

This follows because Alloy reads a join with a predicate as a call with the left side as its first argument.

#### @spec a-box-join-of-a-field-is-said-as-the-navigation

> The verbalizer says `f[x]`, for a field `f`, as `x.f`.

This follows because Alloy reads `f[x]` as the join `x.f`.

#### @spec a-call-with-an-expression-is-said-by-the-body-with-the-expression-in-place

> The verbalizer says a call of a predicate with no reading by its body also when an argument is an expression. The expression takes the place of the parameter.

Derives from: [`spec-a-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body`](#spec-a-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body)

This follows because Alloy binds the parameter to the value of the expression, whatever it holds.

#### @spec a-call-with-one-value-is-said-through-a-member-in-the-place-of-the-argument

> The verbalizer says a call of a predicate with a reading and an argument of one value through a member of its type. That member is the one in the argument.

This follows because an argument that holds exactly one value is that value, and the reading says something of one thing in each slot. The declarations make a navigation of `one` fields from a variable one value.

#### @spec a-call-with-an-argument-of-none-or-several-values-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a call of a predicate with a reading, with an argument that can hold none or several values, and names the argument.

This follows because the reading says something of one thing, and the predicate gets every value of the argument at once.

#### @spec a-call-with-an-argument-of-another-type-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a call whose argument is of a type that shares no member with the type of its parameter, and names both types.

This follows because Alloy rejects such a call as a type error, so the formula claims nothing. Words for it would claim something.

#### @spec a-let-is-said-with-its-value-in-the-place-of-its-name

> The verbalizer says `let x = e | f` as `f` with `e` in the place of `x`. A `let` of several names puts each value in place, in order.

This follows because a `let` only names a value, and the formula it holds means what it means with the value written out.

#### @spec a-let-whose-value-a-quantifier-of-its-body-would-capture-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a `let` whose body declares a variable with a name that its value uses, and names the variable.

Derives from: [`spec-a-let-is-said-with-its-value-in-the-place-of-its-name`](#spec-a-let-is-said-with-its-value-in-the-place-of-its-name)

This follows because the value put in place would then name the variable of the body, where the `let` names another thing.

#### @spec a-negation-is-said-with-the-negative-reading-of-what-it-negates

> The verbalizer says the negation of a comparison or a call with the negative reading of what it negates.

This follows because the table gives each word a positive and a negative reading so that no sentence needs a clumsy "not".

#### @spec not-before-a-compound-is-said-with-the-not-moved-inward

> The verbalizer says `not` before a list, a rule, an equivalence, a quantifier or a temporal operator as the formula it equals with the `not` moved inward. Where no such formula exists, it says "it is not the case that" before the formula, set apart.

This follows because the negative reading of each clause says the negation in the words of the table. Moving the `not` inward reaches those clauses without changing what the formula claims.

##### @spec not-before-an-and-is-said-as-at-least-one-negation

> The verbalizer says `not (a and b)` as `not a or not b`.

This follows because a run of clauses fails exactly when one of them fails.

##### @spec not-before-an-or-is-said-as-every-negation

> The verbalizer says `not (a or b)` as `not a and not b`.

This follows because a run of alternatives fails exactly when each of them fails.

##### @spec not-before-a-rule-is-said-as-its-condition-and-the-negation-of-its-consequence

> The verbalizer says `not (a implies b)` as `a and not b`.

This follows because a rule fails exactly when its condition holds and its consequence does not.

##### @spec not-before-an-equivalence-is-said-as-exactly-one-of-its-sides

> The verbalizer says `not (a iff b)` as exactly one of `a` and `b` holding.

This follows because an equivalence fails exactly when one side holds and the other does not.

<!-- pass-exactly-one:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `exactly-one` is pass 2 of 18 in the pipeline. It changes 30 of the 1754 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text

```

```text
  it is not the case that:
    the cleanup has run exactly when pulse has disposed owner_1.
```

With it:
