```text
For every cleanup, every owner_1 and every owner_2:
  exactly one of these holds:
    - the cleanup has run
    - pulse has disposed owner_1
```
<!-- pass-exactly-one:end -->

##### @spec not-before-an-else-is-said-as-the-rule-with-each-side-negated

> The verbalizer says `not (c implies a else b)` as `c implies not a else not b`.

This follows because the condition picks one side, and the negation fails the side it picks.

##### @spec not-before-some-or-no-is-said-as-the-other

> The verbalizer says `not some x: T | f` as `no x: T | f`, and `not no x: T | f` as `some x: T | f`.

This follows because `no` is the negation of `some`.

##### @spec not-before-all-is-said-as-some-with-the-body-negated

> The verbalizer says `not all x: T | f` as `some x: T | not f`.

This follows because a claim about every value fails exactly when it fails for one.

##### @spec not-before-always-or-eventually-is-said-as-the-other-with-the-formula-negated

> The verbalizer says `not always f` as `eventually not f`, and `not eventually f` as `always not f`.

This follows because a claim about every later moment fails exactly when it fails at one of them.

##### @spec not-before-historically-or-once-is-said-as-the-other-with-the-formula-negated

> The verbalizer says `not historically f` as `once not f`, and `not once f` as `historically not f`.

This follows because the past operators mirror the future ones.

##### @spec not-before-after-is-said-as-after-with-the-formula-negated

> The verbalizer says `not after f` as `after not f`.

Derives from: [`fact-every-moment-has-a-next-moment`](#fact-every-moment-has-a-next-moment)

This follows because each moment has exactly one next moment, so `f` fails there exactly when `not f` holds there.

##### @spec a-not-with-no-formula-to-move-into-is-said-as-it-is-not-the-case-that

> The verbalizer says `not` before `one`, `lone`, `before` or a binary temporal operator as "it is not the case that", with the formula it negates set apart below it.

This follows because none of these has a negation the words say more simply. Setting the formula apart shows where the negation ends.

#### @spec a-union-on-the-left-is-spelled-out

> The verbalizer says a comparison with a union on its left as one statement for each member of the union. For `in` each statement holds, and for `not in` at least one fails.

This follows because a comparison with a union says it of each member, and the reader should not have to unfold it.

With `not in`, the formula denies that every member is in the set, so one member outside it is enough.

#### @spec a-difference-on-the-right-is-spelled-out

> The verbalizer says a comparison with a difference on its right as: the left side is in the first part and not in the second.

This follows because a difference says the right side holds and the removed part does not, which is two statements.

#### @spec a-disj-quantifier-is-said-with-its-variables-different

> The verbalizer says a quantifier with `disj` as the same quantifier with the condition that its variables are different.

This follows because `disj` says that the variables of one declaration stand for different things, and nothing more.

#### @spec a-difference-as-the-type-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-a-condition

> The verbalizer says a quantifier over `A - B` as a quantifier over `A`, with the condition that the variable is not in `B`. When `B` is a variable, the condition is that the two are different.

This follows because the variable ranges over the members of `A` that are not in `B`, which is the type and the condition together.

#### @spec a-set-with-no-noun-as-the-type-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-a-condition

> The verbalizer says a quantifier over a set `S` with no noun over the signature that holds `S`, with the condition that the variable is in `S`.

Derives from: [`spec-some-or-no-of-a-set-of-things-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-of-its-signature`](#spec-some-or-no-of-a-set-of-things-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-of-its-signature)

This follows because each member of `S` is a member of the signature that holds it. The variable ranges over the members of that signature that are in `S`.

#### @spec an-expression-as-the-type-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-a-condition

> The verbalizer says a quantifier over an expression `e`, such as `all o: c.on | …`, as one over the type of `e`, with the condition that the variable is in `e`.

Derives from: [`spec-a-set-with-no-noun-as-the-type-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-a-condition`](#spec-a-set-with-no-noun-as-the-type-of-a-quantifier-is-said-as-a-condition)

This follows because the variable ranges over the members of `e`, and each is a member of its type.

#### @spec a-disj-after-the-colon-is-said-as-a-disj-before-the-names

> The verbalizer says `x, y: disj T` as it says `disj x, y: T`.

Derives from: [`spec-a-disj-quantifier-is-said-with-its-variables-different`](#spec-a-disj-quantifier-is-said-with-its-variables-different)

This follows because Alloy reads `disj` in either place as the condition that the variables are different.

#### @spec one-before-the-type-of-a-variable-is-said-as-the-type

> The verbalizer says `x: one T`, of a quantifier or of a parameter, as `x: T`.

This follows because `one` is what a declaration means when it names no multiplicity: the variable is one member of `T`.

#### @spec a-variable-that-can-hold-several-things-or-none-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a variable declared `lone`, `some` or `set`, or with an arrow in its type, and says that it can hold none or several things.

This follows because a reading says something of one thing in each slot. The readings give no words for "for every" set of things.

#### @spec private-before-a-variable-of-a-quantifier-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses `private` before a variable of a quantifier, which Alloy does not read.

This follows because the analyzer rejects it, so the formula claims nothing.

#### @spec membership-in-a-navigation-is-said-with-the-reading-of-its-field

> The verbalizer says `x in y.f` and `y in f.x` with the reading of the field `f`, with `y` in its first slot and `x` in its second.

This follows because `x in y.f` holds exactly when `y->x` is in `f`, which is what the reading of the field says.

#### @spec no-or-some-of-a-navigation-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-of-the-type-of-the-field

> The verbalizer says `no y.f` and `some y.f` as `no` or `some` of the type that the field `f` points at. The reading of the field puts that noun beside `y`.

This follows because `no y.f` holds exactly when nothing is in `y.f`, and the field declares what can be.

#### @spec a-transpose-in-a-navigation-is-said-as-the-navigation-the-other-way

> The verbalizer says `y.~f` as `f.y`, and `~f.y` as `y.f`.

Derives from: [`spec-membership-in-a-navigation-is-said-with-the-reading-of-its-field`](#spec-membership-in-a-navigation-is-said-with-the-reading-of-its-field)

This follows because `~f` holds `x->y` exactly when `f` holds `y->x`. A navigation of `~f` from one side reaches what a navigation of `f` from the other side reaches, and the reading of `f` says that.

#### @spec a-pair-in-a-transpose-is-said-the-other-way-round

> The verbalizer says `x->y in ~r` as `y->x in r`.

This follows because `~r` holds `x->y` exactly when `r` holds `y->x`.

#### @spec some-or-no-of-a-set-of-things-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-of-its-signature

> The verbalizer says `some S` and `no S`, for a set `S` whose reading takes a variable, as `some` or `no` of the signature that holds `S`. That signature is the one `S` is declared `in` or `extends`, or `S` itself when it stands on its own.

This follows because `some S` holds exactly when a member of that signature is in `S`, and the reading of `S` says what being in `S` is.

##### @spec a-set-whose-reading-says-its-variable-once-is-said-with-a-noun-phrase-in-its-place

> When the reading of `S` says its variable once, the verbalizer puts a noun phrase of the signature in its place: "an edge is being delivered".

This follows because the phrase names the one member that the reading is about, in the one place the reading says it.

##### @spec a-set-whose-reading-says-its-variable-twice-is-said-in-full

> When the reading of `S` says its variable more than once, the verbalizer says `some S` and `no S` in full: a quantifier over the signature, with a numbered name.

This follows because a noun phrase in two places would read as two things, where the logic has one.

##### @spec a-set-with-no-one-signature-that-holds-it-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses `some S` and `no S`, for a set `S` whose reading takes a variable, when the vocabulary declares no one signature that holds `S`, and names `S`.

This follows because without the signature the verbalizer has no noun for the members of `S`, and any noun it chose would be invented.

#### @spec a-primed-name-with-no-reading-of-its-own-is-said-at-the-next-moment

> The verbalizer says a clause that primes one set or field as "at the next moment" and the clause without the prime. A reading of the primed name wins.

This follows because a variable is the same thing at every moment. The primed name is then the only part of the clause that the next moment changes.

#### @spec two-sets-compared-are-said-member-by-member

> The verbalizer says two sets or two relations compared with `in`, `=` or `!=` member by member, over the types of their columns.

This follows because `Ran in Registered` holds exactly when every member of `Ran` is in `Registered`, and a reading says that of one member at a time. A frame condition such as `Registered' = Registered + c` reads this way too.

#### @spec a-field-of-pairs-has-the-types-of-its-columns

> The verbalizer takes the types of the columns of a field declared with an arrow from its declaration, as `older: Cleanup -> Cleanup` of `Clock`.

This follows because the verbalizer says a comparison of such a field, such as `Clock.older' = Clock.older`, over its tuples. Without the types of its columns, the verbalizer would refuse it, and every predicate that keeps it unchanged.

#### @spec membership-in-an-else-of-sets-is-said-through-each-branch

> The verbalizer says `x in (c implies a else b)` as a rule with an "otherwise": when `c`, `x` is in `a`, and otherwise `x` is in `b`.

This follows because an else of sets is `a` where `c` holds and `b` where it does not.

#### @spec an-integer-in-a-number-is-said-as-equal-to-it

> The verbalizer says `y in n`, for a variable `y` that a quantifier declares an integer and a number `n`, as `y = n`.

This follows because a number is one integer, so to be in it is to equal it. Of a variable whose type it does not know, the verbalizer still refuses it.

#### @spec all-or-some-over-a-union-of-signatures-is-said-over-each

> The verbalizer says `all`, `some` or `no` of one variable over a union of signatures that no one type holds as the same quantifier over each signature.

This follows because a formula holds for every member of `A + B` exactly when it holds for every member of each. `some` is the same with "or". The verbalizer refuses `one` and `lone` over such a union, because they do not split that way.

#### @spec sides-that-alloy-does-not-compare-are-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a comparison of sides that hold tuples of different sizes, or things of types that share no member.

This follows because Alloy rejects such a comparison as a type error, so it claims nothing. Words for it would claim something.

#### @spec an-equality-with-a-side-of-unknown-type-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses `=` or `!=` between two sets when the vocabulary does not tell the type of a side that is not a variable.

This follows because the words say the equality over the type of a side. Members of the other side outside that type would go unsaid.

#### @spec a-field-of-one-value-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-with-its-reading

> The verbalizer says `x.f = y` and `x.f != y`, for a field `f` that the vocabulary declares `one` or `lone`, with the reading of the field.

This follows because a field of at most one value equals `y` exactly when `y` is in it.

#### @spec a-field-of-many-values-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-member-by-member

> Take a field `f` that can hold more than one value, where its reading with `y` is more than one plain clause. The verbalizer says `x.f = y` member by member. For every member of the type of `f`, it says the reading of `f` "exactly when" the member and `y` are the same. It says `x.f != y` as the negation of that.

This follows because a set equals `y` when `y` is in it and nothing else is. The reading of the field says only the first half. Where the reading is one plain clause, [`spec-a-set-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-as-the-variable-and-no-other`](#spec-a-set-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-as-the-variable-and-no-other) says both halves in a sentence.

#### @spec a-set-equal-to-a-variable-is-said-as-the-variable-and-no-other

> Take a variable `x`, and a set or a field of many values `s`, where being in `s` is one plain clause. The verbalizer says `s = x` as `x` in `s` "and" no other member of its type in `s`: "the cleanup is on owner_1 and is on no other owner". The second half drops a subject the two share.

This follows because a set equals `x` when `x` is in it and nothing else is, and the two halves say just that. "No other" alone hints that `x` is in the set, which [`spec-no-with-another-is-said-in-full`](#spec-no-with-another-is-said-in-full) guards against. Here the first half says it, so the hint is true. A plain clause keeps "no other" at the level of the claim. Inside a noun phrase, as in "an owner that no other owner is the parent of", it would cover less.

<!-- pass-x-and-no-other:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `x-and-no-other` is pass 4 of 18 in the pipeline. It changes 22 of the 1754 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup, s: String | c.tags = "a"
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup, every text_1 and every text_2:
  the cleanup is tagged text_2 exactly when text_2 and "a" are the same.
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup and every text_1:
  the cleanup is tagged "a" and is tagged no other text.
```

- Readers: A strict judge (Opus) found 46 of 46 changed statements lossless; two haiku readers got 16 of 16 situations right, "no other" over an empty set among them.
- Rejected: "no other" inside a noun phrase, as in "an owner that no other owner is the parent of": it covers less than the claim.
- Rejected: a field of at most one value: its reading already says it, "owner_1 is the home of the cleanup".
<!-- pass-x-and-no-other:end -->

#### @spec two-values-that-are-equal-are-said-member-by-member

> The verbalizer says `y.f = z.g` as "for every" member of the type of `f`, the reading of `f` "exactly when" the reading of `g`. When one side is primed, it says that side "at the next moment" and the other "now". It says `y.f != z.g` as the negation of that.

This follows because two sets are equal exactly when they have the same members. The type of the field holds every member that either side can have.

#### @spec an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns

> The verbalizer says a formula about an expression through members of the types of its columns. This holds for an expression that is more than a set or a navigation of a variable.

This follows because the vocabulary declares the types of what an expression can hold. A claim about what it holds is then a claim about each member of those types, which the readings say.

##### @spec a-union-on-the-right-is-said-as-or

> The verbalizer says `x in a + b`, for a variable or a pair `x`, as `x in a` or `x in b`.

This follows because a member of a union is a member of one of its parts.

##### @spec an-intersection-on-the-right-is-said-as-and

> The verbalizer says `x in a & b`, for a variable or a pair `x`, as `x in a` and `x in b`.

This follows because a member of an intersection is a member of both of its parts.

##### @spec not-in-before-a-difference-is-said-as-the-negation-of-in

> The verbalizer says `x not in a - b` as the negation of `x in a - b`: `x not in a` or `x in b`.

This follows because `not in` is the negation of `in`.

##### @spec membership-in-a-navigation-of-an-expression-is-said-as-a-pair-in-it

> The verbalizer says `x in y.e`, for a variable `y`, as `y->x in e`, and `x in e.y` as `x->y in e`.

This follows because `y` is one thing, so `y.e` holds what `e` pairs with `y`.

##### @spec a-pair-in-a-product-is-said-as-each-side-in-its-part

> The verbalizer says `x->y in a -> b` as `x in a` and `y in b`.

This follows because a product holds every pair of a member of `a` and a member of `b`, and nothing else.

##### @spec membership-in-a-chain-of-navigations-is-said-through-a-member-between

> The verbalizer says `x in e.f`, where `e` is not one variable, as `some m: T | m in e and x in m.f`. `T` is the type of the last column of `e`.

This follows because `e.f` holds what `f` gives a member of `e`, and every member of `e` is a member of `T`.

##### @spec membership-in-a-navigation-from-a-signature-is-said-through-a-member-of-it

> The verbalizer says `x in S.f`, for a signature `S` where `S.f` has no reading of its own, as `some m: S | m->x in f`: "a cleanup is on x".

This follows because `S.f` holds what `f` gives some member of `S`.

##### @spec membership-in-a-signature-with-no-reading-is-said-with-its-noun

> The verbalizer says `x in S`, for a signature `S` with a noun and no reading, as `x` "is" the noun with its article: "c is a cleanup".

This follows because to be in a signature is to be one of its kind, which its noun names.

##### @spec a-primed-expression-is-said-at-the-next-moment

> The verbalizer says `x in e'`, for an expression `e`, as "at the next moment" before `x in e`.

This follows because a variable is the same thing at every moment, so the prime moves only `e`.

##### @spec an-expression-of-a-variable-on-the-left-is-said-member-by-member

> The verbalizer says `e in s`, for an expression `e` that names a variable, as: for every member `m` of the type of `e`, when `m in e`, `m in s`.

This follows because one set is in another exactly when each of its members is.

##### @spec two-expressions-that-are-equal-are-said-member-by-member

> The verbalizer says `a = b`, for sides that the specs above do not say, as: for every member `m` of their type, `m in a` exactly when `m in b`. It says `a != b` as the negation of that.

This follows because two sets are equal exactly when they have the same members.

##### @spec some-or-no-of-an-expression-is-said-over-the-types-of-its-columns

> The verbalizer says `some e` and `no e`, for an expression the specs above do not say, as `some` or `no` over its column types, with the members in `e`.

This follows because an expression holds something exactly when some members of its types are in it.

##### @spec one-or-lone-of-an-expression-is-said-as-exactly-or-at-most-one

> The verbalizer says `one e` and `lone e` as exactly one or at most one member of the types of the columns of `e` in `e`.

This follows because `one e` holds when `e` holds one member, and `lone e` when it holds at most one.

##### @spec an-expression-whose-types-the-vocabulary-does-not-tell-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a formula about an expression whose column types the vocabulary does not tell, and names the expression.

This follows because a member of a type the verbalizer guessed could leave out what the expression holds.

#### @spec an-override-is-said-as-the-pairs-of-its-right-and-the-rest-of-its-left

> The verbalizer says `x->y in r ++ s` as `x->y in s`, or `x->y in r` and `no x.s`. For sets, `x in a ++ b` is `x in a + b`.

Derives from: [`spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns`](#spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns)

This follows because an override keeps the pairs of `s` and the pairs of `r` whose first member `s` relates to nothing. A set relates nothing, so its override is its union.

#### @spec a-domain-restriction-is-said-as-the-first-member-in-the-set

> The verbalizer says `x->y in a <: r` as `x in a` and `x->y in r`.

Derives from: [`spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns`](#spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns)

This follows because `a <: r` keeps the pairs of `r` whose first member is in `a`.

#### @spec a-range-restriction-is-said-as-the-last-member-in-the-set

> The verbalizer says `x->y in r :> b` as `x->y in r` and `y in b`.

Derives from: [`spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns`](#spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns)

This follows because `r :> b` keeps the pairs of `r` whose last member is in `b`.

#### @spec an-arrow-with-a-multiplicity-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses an arrow with a multiplicity, such as `a one -> lone b`, and says that it says how many each side relates.

This follows because a multiplicity on an arrow says how many things a relation pairs with each member, and no reading says that.

#### @spec a-closure-is-said-as-reaching-in-one-or-more-steps

> The verbalizer says `x->y in ^r` as `x` "reaches" `y` "in one or more steps", and says what a step is with the reading of `r`.

Derives from: [`spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns`](#spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns)

This follows because `^r` holds `x->y` exactly when a chain of pairs of `r` leads from `x` to `y`.

#### @spec a-reflexive-closure-is-said-as-reaching-in-zero-or-more-steps

> The verbalizer says `x->y in *r` as `x` "reaches" `y` "in zero or more steps", and says what a step is with the reading of `r`.

Derives from: [`spec-a-closure-is-said-as-reaching-in-one-or-more-steps`](#spec-a-closure-is-said-as-reaching-in-one-or-more-steps)

This follows because `*r` is `^r` with every member paired with itself, which a chain of no steps reaches.

#### @spec some-or-no-of-a-reflexive-closure-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses `some`, `no`, `one` or `lone` of a reflexive closure, and says that it holds every member of every type.

This follows because `*r` pairs every atom with itself, Int atoms included, and no type the vocabulary declares holds them all.

#### @spec none-is-said-as-nothing

> The verbalizer says `e = none`, `none = e` and `e in none` as `no e`, and `e != none` as `some e`. It leaves `none` out of a union or a difference, and says `x in none` alone as never holding. It takes `none in e`, and a quantifier over `none` but `some` and `one`, as always holding, and says `#none` as 0.

This follows because `none` holds nothing.

#### @spec a-quantifier-over-a-variable-is-said-of-the-variable

> The verbalizer says `all x: p | f` and `some x: p | f`, for a variable `p`, as `f` with `p` in the place of `x`, and `no x: p | f` as its negation.

This follows because a variable holds one thing, so a quantifier over it ranges over that thing alone. `lone x: p | f` always holds.

#### @spec a-value-in-its-own-builtin-type-always-holds

> The verbalizer takes a string in `String`, and an integer variable in `Int`, as a formula that always holds.

This follows because a value is always in its own type. Alone such a formula claims nothing, and in an `and` it changes nothing.

#### @spec a-formula-that-never-holds-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a formula that never holds, such as `some none`, and says that it claims what cannot be.

This follows because no words of the readings say a formula that is always false, and words that seemed to would hide it.

#### @spec a-formula-that-never-holds-is-left-out-of-an-or

> The verbalizer leaves a formula that never holds, such as `x in none`, out of an `or`.

This follows because `a or false` claims what `a` claims.

#### @spec a-pair-in-iden-is-said-as-the-same

> The verbalizer says `x->y in iden` as `x` and `y` being the same.

This follows because `iden` pairs each atom with itself, and nothing else.

#### @spec univ-is-said-as-a-signature-of-its-own

> The verbalizer says `univ` as a signature that holds every atom, with the noun the readings give it.

This follows because `univ` is the set of every atom, a signature that no declaration names. Without a noun of its own, a quantifier over it is refused as any type with no noun is.

#### @spec a-set-comprehension-is-said-through-its-variables

> The verbalizer says `x in { y: T | f }` as `x in T` and `f` with `x` in the place of `y`, and `{ y: T }` as `T`.

Derives from: [`spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns`](#spec-an-expression-is-said-through-the-types-of-its-columns)

This follows because the comprehension holds the members of `T` for which `f` holds.

#### @spec disj-of-expressions-is-said-as-no-two-sharing-a-member

> The verbalizer says `disj[a, b]` as `a` and `b` being different when both are variables, and as `no a & b` otherwise. Over more arguments, it says it of each pair.

This follows because `disj` holds when no two of its arguments share a member.

#### @spec a-string-is-said-as-itself-in-quotes

> The verbalizer says a string in the place of a variable as itself, in quotes: "c is named "abc"".

This follows because a string is one thing, and its quotes show the reader where it starts and ends.

#### @spec an-expression-is-one-thing-where-its-declarations-make-it-so

> The verbalizer takes an expression for one thing only where the declarations make it so. That covers a variable, a string and a number. It also covers a navigation of a `one` field from one thing, and such an expression primed.

This follows because a rewrite that takes an expression for one thing is lossless only when it holds exactly one. The kind of syntax does not tell that: `c.name` is one thing when `name` is a `one` field, and `c.tags` is not when `tags` is a `set` field.

#### @spec a-variable-a-quantifier-declares-has-the-type-it-declares

> In the types of the columns of an expression, the verbalizer takes a variable to be of the type its quantifier declares.

This follows because an expression such as `on ++ (c -> o)` has the types of `on` only if `c` and `o` have them too. Without them, the verbalizer would refuse an override that updates a state.

#### @spec a-variable-on-the-right-of-in-is-said-as-equal-to-what-is-in-it

> The verbalizer says `x in p`, for a variable `p` that a quantifier declares, as `x = p` where `x` is one thing. Where `x` can hold several things, it says that each of them is `p`.

This follows because a variable holds one thing, so what is in it is that thing. A name that no quantifier declares is not known to hold one thing, and is still refused when it has no reading.

#### @spec some-or-no-of-a-signature-is-said-over-its-members

> The verbalizer says `some S`, `no S`, `one S` and `lone S` of a signature `S` with a noun and no reading by its noun alone, as `there is an owner`.

This follows because `some S` claims that `S` has a member, and the noun of `S` names one. The words need no variable.

#### @spec a-count-of-one-thing-is-a-formula-that-always-or-never-holds

> The verbalizer takes `some`, `one` and `lone` of one thing as a formula that always holds, and `no` of one thing as one that never does.

This follows because one thing is exactly one. The verbalizer leaves such a formula out of an `and` or an `or` where it changes nothing. Alone, it refuses it, as it refuses the other formulas that always or never hold.

#### @spec a-value-in-a-string-is-said-as-equal-to-it

> The verbalizer says `x in "a"`, where `x` is [one thing](#spec-an-expression-is-one-thing-where-its-declarations-make-it-so), as `x = "a"`: "c and "a" are the same". It says `x not in "a"` as `x != "a"`.

Derives from: [`spec-a-string-is-said-as-itself-in-quotes`](#spec-a-string-is-said-as-itself-in-quotes)

This follows because `x` is one thing and a string is one thing, so `x` is in the string exactly when the two are the same. A left side that can hold none or several things is not one thing: `c.tags in "a"` holds when `c.tags` is empty, and `c.tags = "a"` does not. The verbalizer says such a side member by member, as [`spec-an-expression-of-a-variable-on-the-left-is-said-member-by-member`](#spec-an-expression-of-a-variable-on-the-left-is-said-member-by-member) says.

#### @spec set-or-seq-before-an-expression-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses `set e` and `seq e` as a formula, and says that Alloy reads them only in a declaration.

This follows because the analyzer does not read either as a formula, so neither claims anything.

#### @spec a-rule-of-two-clauses-is-said-on-one-line

<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-of-two-clauses-is-said-on-one-line:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When all of these hold:
> - a [list](#term-series) is a rule whose two sides are each one clause
> - the list is not a rule whose first side begins with a time phrase
>
> then [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list on one line, as "when" the first side, the second side.
<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-of-two-clauses-is-said-on-one-line:end -->

A short rule reads best as one sentence: "when this, that". So when each side of a rule is a single clause, the verbalizer puts the rule on one line. This holds only when the first side does not open with a time phrase.

```alloy
all f: Series | (f in OneLineRule and f not in TimeFirst) implies f in OneLine
```

<!-- pass-rule-on-one-line:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `rule-on-one-line` is pass 15 of 18 in the pipeline. It changes 268 of the 1754 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup | c in Ran implies c in Registered
```

Without the pass:

```text
When a cleanup has run
then code has registered the cleanup.
```

With it:

```text
When a cleanup has run, code has registered the cleanup.
```
<!-- pass-rule-on-one-line:end -->

#### @spec an-equivalence-of-two-clauses-is-said-with-exactly-when

> The verbalizer says `a iff b`, when each side is one clause, as `a` "exactly when" `b`.

This follows because "exactly when" says that each side holds when the other does, which is what `iff` claims.

<!-- pass-exactly-when:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `exactly-when` is pass 14 of 18 in the pipeline. It changes 40 of the 1754 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup, o, p: Owner | (c in Ran iff o in Disposed)
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup, every owner_1 and every owner_2:
  both or neither of these hold:
    - the cleanup has run
    - pulse has disposed owner_1
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup, every owner_1 and every owner_2:
  the cleanup has run exactly when pulse has disposed owner_1.
```
<!-- pass-exactly-when:end -->

#### @spec an-equivalence-of-more-than-clauses-is-said-as-both-or-neither

> The verbalizer says `a iff b`, when a side is more than one clause, as a list of the two sides under "both or neither of these hold".

This follows because "exactly when" between two lists or rules would not show where each side ends.

#### @spec an-equivalence-that-is-a-side-of-a-rule-is-said-as-both-or-neither

> As a side of a rule, of a binary temporal operator or of a definition, the verbalizer says `a iff b` as both or neither.

This follows because "exactly when" inside "when …, …", or after the "exactly when" of a definition, could take the whole sentence as its side.

#### @spec an-equivalence-whose-first-side-begins-with-a-time-phrase-is-said-as-both-or-neither

> The verbalizer says `a iff b` as both or neither of its sides when `a` begins with a time phrase. A clause at the next moment and a clause now are the exception.

This follows because the time phrase at the start would read as covering both sides, where the formula has it cover `a`.

#### @spec a-clause-at-the-next-moment-equal-to-a-clause-now-is-said-with-exactly-when

> The verbalizer says `a' iff b`, for clauses with no other time phrase, comma, "and", "or" or relative clause, as `a` "at the next moment exactly when" `b` "now".

This follows because the time phrase then ends its own clause, and "now" marks the other. Neither can reach across "exactly when". A frame condition such as `Ran' = Ran` reads this way, member by member.

#### @spec an-equivalence-whose-first-side-holds-a-noun-phrase-is-said-as-both-or-neither

> The verbalizer says `a iff b` as both or neither of its sides when `a` holds a noun phrase, such as "no owner".

This follows because "exactly when" follows `a` with no comma between. A reader could take it as part of the noun phrase, "no owner exactly when …", where the formula has it join the two sides.

#### @spec an-else-is-said-as-otherwise

> The verbalizer says `c implies a else b` as the rule "when" `c`, `a`, with "otherwise" before `b`.

This follows because `b` is claimed exactly when `c` does not hold, which is what "otherwise" says.

#### @spec a-sentence-starts-with-a-capital-only-where-it-starts-with-its-own-words

> A statement begins with a capital where it begins with its own words, and with the name unchanged where it begins with a name.

This follows because a name from the formula, such as a variable, stays as it is.

#### @spec two-variables-are-said-to-be-different-or-the-same

> The verbalizer says a comparison of two variables as "different" or "the same".

This follows because the logic compares two things, and the reader should hear that they are two, or one.

#### @spec eventually-is-said-as-now-or-later

> The verbalizer says `eventually` as "now or later".

This follows because eventually includes the present moment, and "someday" or "sooner or later" would leave it out. "Now or later" names both, in the words people use.

#### @spec after-is-said-as-at-the-next-moment

> The verbalizer says `after` as "at the next moment".

This follows because after looks one step ahead and no further.

#### @spec always-is-said-as-from-now-on

> The verbalizer says `always` as "from now on", unless what it covers is a rule.

This follows because always holds from the present on, the present included. "At every moment" would also reach back to the moments before it, which historically covers.

#### @spec a-rule-at-every-later-moment-is-said-from-now-on-whenever

> The verbalizer says `always` over a rule as "from now on, whenever" the rule's condition, followed by its consequence.

This follows because a rule that holds at every moment is what "whenever" means in plain English. "From now on" keeps the start at the present, as `always` alone does. So the words still leave the moments before it out.

<!-- pass-always-inside-for-every:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `always-inside-for-every` is pass 3 of 18 in the pipeline. It changes 7 of the 1754 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
always all c: Cleanup | c in Registered implies c in Ran
```

Without the pass:

```text
From now on, for every cleanup:
  when code has registered the cleanup, the cleanup has run.
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup:
  from now on, whenever code has registered the cleanup, the cleanup has run.
```
<!-- pass-always-inside-for-every:end -->

<!-- pass-from-now-on-whenever:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `from-now-on-whenever` is pass 16 of 18 in the pipeline. It changes 8 of the 1754 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
always all c: Cleanup | c in Registered implies c in Ran
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup:
  from now on:
    when code has registered the cleanup, the cleanup has run.
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup:
  from now on, whenever code has registered the cleanup, the cleanup has run.
```

- Readers: Two passes of a strict judge (Opus) found 98 of 102 sampled statements lossless; the 4 failures came from the old "a moment before", now "a moment just before".
- Readers: On a canon of 41 rules, a judge rated 25 as reading as well as the handwritten claim, against none before.
- Rejected: "whenever" over a rule that says "now" or a moment before: its "now" would count from each moment "whenever" picks.
<!-- pass-from-now-on-whenever:end -->

#### @spec before-is-said-as-there-is-a-moment-just-before-and-at-it

> The verbalizer says `before` as `there is a moment just before, and at it`.

This follows because before looks one step back, and fails at the first moment, which has no moment before it. "At the moment before" would leave that out, and "a moment before" alone would read as any earlier moment, which once covers.

#### @spec once-is-said-as-now-or-earlier

> The verbalizer says `once` as "now or earlier".

This follows because once is eventually turned to the past, and includes the present moment as eventually does.

#### @spec historically-is-said-as-now-and-at-every-earlier-moment

> The verbalizer says `historically` as "now and at every earlier moment".

This follows because historically is always turned to the past, and includes the present moment as always does.

#### @spec a-sequence-is-said-as-and-at-the-next-moment

> The verbalizer says `a ; b` as "a, and at the next moment, b".

This follows because the semicolon says that the first side holds now and the second side holds at the next moment.

#### @spec a-time-phrase-before-words-that-hold-a-time-phrase-sets-them-apart

> Before words with a time phrase of their own, the verbalizer ends a time phrase with a colon and sets the words apart below it.

This follows because two time phrases in a row, such as "from now on, at the next moment", read as one moment. A reader could also take a second "at the next moment" later in the words as the moment of the first.

<!-- pass-time-phrase-in-front:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `time-phrase-in-front` is pass 11 of 18 in the pipeline. It changes 347 of the 1754 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
always all c: Cleanup | c in Ran
```

Without the pass:

```text
From now on:
  for every cleanup:
    the cleanup has run.
```

With it:

```text
From now on, for every cleanup:
  the cleanup has run.
```
<!-- pass-time-phrase-in-front:end -->

#### @spec an-and-or-an-or-below-a-time-phrase-is-a-list

> The verbalizer says an "and" or an "or" that a time phrase covers as a list below it, and never as one sentence after it.

This follows because in "at the next moment, a or b" a reader can take the time phrase as covering `a` alone, with `b` read as now. As a heading over a list, the phrase covers every item.

#### @spec the-spellings-of-not-in-and-not-equal-are-said-alike

> The verbalizer says `!in`, `! in`, `not =` and `! =` as it says `not in` and `!=`.

This follows because Alloy reads each spelling as the same comparison.

#### @spec text-that-alloy-does-not-read-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a formula that Alloy does not read, such as `a == b`, with the reason the parser gives.

This follows because a formula the analyzer cannot read claims nothing, so no words can say it.

#### @spec a-binary-temporal-operator-is-said-with-its-sides-set-apart

> The verbalizer sets each side of `until`, `since`, `releases` and `triggered` apart when either side is more than one plain clause, and each side of `;` that is. It puts them below the words that place them in time.

This follows because each operator bounds a stretch of moments by a moment where a side holds. On one line, the words name that moment as "the first moment where" or "the last moment where". A reader can count such a moment from the start of the run, or past now. Set apart, the moment is "the first such moment" after one counted from now, and the stretch says where it starts and ends. A longer side set apart also shows where it ends.

##### @spec until-is-said-as-two-parts

> When a side is more than one plain clause, the verbalizer says `a until b` in two parts. First comes `b` "now or later", then `a` "at every moment from now until the first such moment, not including it".

This follows because until claims that `b` comes, now or later, and that `a` holds at every moment before it first does.

##### @spec since-is-said-as-two-parts

> When a side is more than one plain clause, the verbalizer says `a since b` in two parts. First comes `b` "now or earlier", then `a` "at every moment after the last such moment, up to and including now".

This follows because since is until turned to the past.

##### @spec until-of-two-plain-clauses-is-one-sentence

> The verbalizer says `a until b` of two plain clauses as one sentence: `b` "now or later, and until then," `a`.

This follows because a plain clause holds no time phrase, comma or relative clause. So "now or later" can only cover `b`, and "then" can only be a moment of `b` counted from now. "Until then" stops before that moment, as until does, and readers of every size took it that way.

<!-- pass-until-in-a-sentence:begin — generated by `node test/core/wordings.ts --write`; edits are overwritten -->
The pass `until-in-a-sentence` is pass 10 of 18 in the pipeline. It changes 40 of the 1754 formulas of the sweep.

The shortest of them, as written in Alloy:

```text
all c: Cleanup, o, p: Owner | (c in Ran until o in Disposed)
```

Without the pass:

```text
For every cleanup, every owner_1 and every owner_2:
  all of these hold:
    - now or later, the following holds:
        pulse has disposed owner_1
    - at every moment from now until the first such moment, not including it, the following holds:
        the cleanup has run.
```

With it:

```text
For every cleanup, every owner_1 and every owner_2:
  pulse has disposed owner_1 now or later, and until then, the cleanup has run.
```

- Readers: On 8 timelines built to catch each misreading, 5 of 5 readers (Opus, Sonnet, three haiku) read "until then" right; "first" is not needed, since any moment of b gives the same truth.
- Rejected: "up to the first such moment, but not necessarily at it": lossless, and longer than it needs to be.
- Rejected: "ever since", "since then" and "after that" for since: each misread by a haiku reader, as counting the moment of b itself or as its first moment; since needs the last.
<!-- pass-until-in-a-sentence:end -->

##### @spec since-of-two-plain-clauses-is-one-sentence

> Of two plain clauses, the verbalizer says `a since b` as one sentence. It says `b` "now or earlier", then `a` "at every moment after the last such moment, up to and including now".

This follows because since is until turned to the past, and the same plain clauses leave its words one reading. "Ever since" would read as covering the moment of `b` too, so the words name the stretch in full.

##### @spec releases-is-said-as-always-or-until

> The verbalizer says `a releases b` as `always b or (b until (a and b))`.

This follows because releases holds `b` up to and including the first moment where `a` holds, and for ever when that moment never comes. The two alternatives say each case.

##### @spec triggered-is-said-as-historically-or-since

> The verbalizer says `a triggered b` as `historically b or (b since (a and b))`.

This follows because triggered is releases turned to the past.

##### @spec a-sequence-with-a-side-of-more-than-a-clause-is-said-as-and-at-the-next-moment

> The verbalizer says `a ; b`, with a side that is more than one plain clause, as `a and after b`.

This follows because `a ; b` claims `a` now and `b` at the next moment, which `a and after b` claims too.

##### @spec a-side-with-a-time-phrase-a-noun-phrase-or-a-where-is-more-than-a-plain-clause

> A side is one plain clause only when the verbalizer says it by one reading with a variable in each of its places. It holds no time phrase, no comma, no noun phrase, no relative clause, no "where" and no "it is not the case that".

This follows because the words cannot mark the reach of any of these inline. After "c is on no owner", "now or later" could cover the whole side. It could also cover only "is on", which says that c is on no owner at every later moment. After "c has run or pulse has disposed o", it could cover only the last alternative.

#### @spec this-outside-a-definition-of-a-signature-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses `this` outside a predicate or a function of a signature, which Alloy does not read.

This follows because the analyzer finds no name `this` there, so the formula claims nothing.

#### @spec steps-in-a-formula-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses `steps` in a formula, and says that Alloy reads it only in a scope.

This follows because the analyzer finds no name `steps` in a formula.

#### @spec a-name-of-this-module-is-said-as-the-name

> The verbalizer says `this/Ran` and `@Ran` as it says `Ran`.

This follows because `this/` names the module the formula is in, and outside the fact of a signature, `@` changes nothing.

#### @spec a-name-of-another-module-is-said-by-its-own-reading

> The verbalizer says a name of another module, such as `m/Ran`, by the reading of that whole name.

This follows because two modules may each have a `Ran`, and the reading of one would not say the other.

#### @spec a-comment-in-a-formula-is-left-out

> The verbalizer leaves out a comment in a formula: `--`, `//`, `/* … */` and `/** … */`.

This follows because Alloy reads a comment as nothing, so it claims nothing.

#### @spec a-typographic-prime-is-said-as-a-prime

> The verbalizer says `‘` and `’` as it says `'`.

This follows because Alloy reads all three as the prime.

#### @spec an-integer-comparison-is-said-in-integers-that-wrap

> The verbalizer says `<`, `>`, `=<`, `>=` and their negations, and `=` and `!=` between two numbers, after "in integers that wrap around at the analyzer's bit width".

Derives from: [`fact-the-analyzer-wraps-integers-at-their-bit-width`](#fact-the-analyzer-wraps-integers-at-their-bit-width)

This follows because the words of arithmetic say what the analyzer computes only when the reader knows that its integers wrap around.

##### @spec two-numbers-are-compared-with-the-words-of-their-operator

> The verbalizer says `<` as "is less than", `>` as "is greater than", `=<` as "is at most", `>=` as "is at least" and `=` as "is equal to". It says a negation with "not".

This follows because those words say the order of two numbers, and the words before them say the wrap once.

##### @spec a-count-is-said-as-the-number-of-values

> The verbalizer says `#e` as "the number of values of" a member of the type of `e`, "such that" the member is in `e`.

This follows because `#e` counts the members of `e`.

##### @spec a-sum-over-a-variable-is-said-as-the-sum-over-every-value

> The verbalizer says `sum x: T | e` as "the sum, over every" member of `T`, "of" `e`.

This follows because the sum adds the value of `e` for each member of `T`.

##### @spec a-set-of-integers-where-a-number-belongs-is-said-as-the-sum-of-its-members

> The verbalizer says a set of integers where a number belongs, as in `c.n < 3` or `int[c.n]`, as `"the sum of the values of"` an integer in it.

This follows because the analyzer reads a set of integers where a number belongs as the sum of its members, as `int` says.

##### @spec plus-minus-and-mul-are-said-as-plus-minus-and-times

> The verbalizer says `plus[a, b]`, `minus[a, b]` and `mul[a, b]` as `a` "plus", "minus" or "times" `b`.

This follows because those are the words of the operations, and the comparison says that they wrap.

##### @spec a-division-is-said-with-its-rounding-and-its-rule-for-zero

> The verbalizer says `div[a, b]` as `a` "divided by" `b`, rounded toward zero, with its value when `b` is zero. It says `rem[a, b]` as `"the remainder of"` `a` divided by `b`, with its sign and its value when `b` is zero.

Derives from: [`fact-the-analyzer-divides-toward-zero-and-gives-the-sign-for-zero`](#fact-the-analyzer-divides-toward-zero-and-gives-the-sign-for-zero)

This follows because the analyzer divides by zero, and rounds, in ways that ordinary words for division leave open.

##### @spec a-number-is-said-as-itself

> The verbalizer says a number in decimal, whether the formula writes it in decimal, in hexadecimal or in binary.

This follows because the value is what the formula claims, and the comparison says that it wraps.

##### @spec min-and-max-are-said-as-the-least-and-the-greatest-integer

> The verbalizer says `min` and `max` as "the least integer" and "the greatest integer".

This follows because they are the ends of the range that the bit width gives.

##### @spec the-spellings-fun-min-fun-max-and-fun-next-are-said-as-min-max-and-next

> The verbalizer says `fun/min`, `fun/max` and `fun/next` as it says `min`, `max` and `next`.

This follows because the analyzer reads each spelling as the same integer or relation. A spelling said as its name would leave the reader without its meaning.

##### @spec a-part-of-an-integer-comparison-that-is-more-than-a-number-is-named-below-it

> The verbalizer names a count, a sum or a division in an integer comparison as `number_1`, `number_2` and so on, and says after "where" what each is.

This follows because the words of a count end in a clause of their own. Two of them in one sentence would read two ways.

##### @spec a-shift-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses `<<`, `>>` and `>>>`, and says that the analyzer shifts by the lowest bits of the amount.

Derives from: [`fact-the-analyzer-shifts-by-the-lowest-bits-of-the-amount`](#fact-the-analyzer-shifts-by-the-lowest-bits-of-the-amount)

This follows because words for a shift by an amount the bits do not hold would have to count bits. Plain words would say a different shift.

##### @spec a-set-compared-with-a-number-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses `=` and `!=` between a set and a number, such as `c.n = 2`, and names them.

This follows because Alloy reads them as sets, which compare the set with the one integer of the number. The words would have to say both the sets and the wrap of the number.

##### @spec a-number-outside-an-integer-comparison-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a number or a count outside an integer comparison, and names it.

This follows because outside a comparison, the number is an integer atom of the analyzer's range. No words there say that it wraps.

#### @spec the-next-integer-is-said-as-the-integer-after

> The verbalizer says `x->y in next` as `y` "is the integer after" `x` "without wrapping around".

This follows because `next` pairs each integer with the one after it, and the greatest integer with none. Integer arithmetic wraps, and the words of a comparison say so. Without the last words, the integer after the greatest would read as the least.

#### @spec int-and-seq-int-have-nouns-of-their-own

> The verbalizer says `Int` with the noun "integer", and `seq/Int` with the noun "sequence index", unless the readings give another.

This follows because Alloy declares both signatures, so no vocabulary gives them a noun.

#### @spec a-name-with-no-reading-is-refused-and-named

> The verbalizer refuses a formula with a name that has no reading, and names the word.

This follows because a statement that skips the name says less than the logic holds. The author can mend only what the verbalizer names.

#### @spec a-reading-with-no-negative-form-is-refused-and-named

> The verbalizer refuses a formula that negates a word whose reading has no negative form, and names the word.

This follows because the verbalizer would have to invent a negation, and the invention may mean something else.

#### @spec a-type-with-no-noun-is-refused-and-named

> The verbalizer refuses a formula that quantifies a type with no noun, and names the type.

This follows because a quantifier without a noun for its type cannot say what its variable stands for.

#### @spec a-reading-that-uses-a-slot-the-formula-does-not-give-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a formula whose reading of a word uses a place that the formula does not fill, and names the place.

This follows because the reading talks about something the formula does not mention, and any word put there would be invented.

#### @spec a-reading-that-leaves-out-a-slot-the-formula-gives-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a formula whose reading of a word leaves out a place that the formula fills, and names the place.

This follows because the variable in that place would drop out of the statement, which would then say less than the formula.

#### @spec a-binary-temporal-operator-inside-a-side-of-another-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses `until`, `since`, `releases`, `triggered` or `;` with a side that holds one of them, except a `;` after a `;`.

This follows because the words of each one are a clause with commas, and two of them nested read in more than one way. A chain of `;` reads in order, each later step set apart below the "at the next moment" of the one before it.

#### @spec a-primed-relation-of-a-variable-signature-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a prime on a relation `Sig.rel` that has a reading of its own when `Sig` is a `var sig`.

This follows because the prime then moves the signature to the next moment too. "At the next moment" in front would say that, but the reading of the relation names the signature as it is now.

#### @spec a-construct-the-words-do-not-cover-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a formula with a construct that the words do not cover, and names the construct.

This follows because leaving a construct out would hide part of the logic, and guessing its words could change its meaning.

#### @spec a-line-of-readings-that-cannot-be-read-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a [line](#term-line) of readings that has neither a noun nor a key, and says that it cannot read the line.

This follows because a line the verbalizer misreads would give a word the wrong sentence.

#### @spec a-bracket-with-no-partner-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a line of readings with a bracket that has no partner, and says so.

This follows because a bracket marks the word that links to a term, and half a mark would link the wrong words.

#### @spec a-predicate-whose-body-cannot-be-said-is-refused-with-advice-to-give-it-a-reading

> The verbalizer refuses a call of a predicate with no reading and a body the words do not cover, and advises a reading.

This follows because a body the verbalizer cannot say is no fallback, and the reading is how the author mends it.

#### @spec a-predicate-defined-in-terms-of-itself-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a call of a predicate whose body calls that predicate, and says that it calls itself.

This follows because a body that calls itself never ends in words.

#### @spec a-call-with-the-wrong-number-of-arguments-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a call with the wrong number of arguments, and says how many the predicate takes.

This follows because an argument with no parameter, or a parameter with no argument, has no place in the words.

#### @spec text-that-is-not-a-definition-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses text given as a definition that is not one, and says how to write a definition.

This follows because the verbalizer words a definition as one, and text that only looks like a formula would get the wrong words.

#### @spec a-parameter-with-no-type-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a definition with a parameter that has no type, and says so.

This follows because the statement says "for every" a noun of the type, and a parameter without a type has no noun.

#### @spec a-definition-whose-body-is-a-rule-is-said-with-the-rule-set-apart

> The verbalizer says a definition whose body is a rule or a "for every" as what it names "exactly when the following holds". It sets the body apart below.

This follows because "exactly when" before a rule on the same line would leave the reader to guess where the body ends.

#### @spec a-definition-of-a-word-with-no-reading-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a definition of a word that has no reading, and names the word.

This follows because the statement of a definition says the word it defines, and without a reading it would say nothing.

#### @spec a-passage-that-starts-with-pred-is-a-definition

> The verbalizer reads text that starts with the keyword `pred` as a definition.

This follows because the keyword is how the author says that the text defines a word.

#### @spec a-passage-that-starts-with-fun-is-a-definition

> The verbalizer reads text that starts with the keyword `fun` as a definition.

Derives from: [`spec-a-passage-that-starts-with-pred-is-a-definition`](#spec-a-passage-that-starts-with-pred-is-a-definition)

This follows because a function defines a word too: the name of its value.

#### @spec private-before-a-definition-changes-nothing-that-is-said

> The verbalizer says a `private pred` or a `private fun` as it says the same definition without `private`.

This follows because `private` says where Alloy lets the name be used, and nothing about what it means.

#### @spec parameters-in-round-brackets-are-read-as-in-square-ones

> The verbalizer reads `pred p(x: T)` as `pred p[x: T]`.

This follows because Alloy reads both brackets alike.

#### @spec a-comma-before-or-after-the-parameters-is-read-as-none

> The verbalizer reads `pred p[, x: T]` and `pred p[x: T,]` as `pred p[x: T]`.

This follows because Alloy reads a comma at either end of the list as nothing.

#### @spec a-predicate-of-a-signature-takes-this-as-its-first-parameter

> The verbalizer reads `pred T.p[x: U] { … }` as `pred p[this: T, x: U] { … }`, for its definition and for a call of it.

This follows because Alloy reads a predicate of a signature as one whose first parameter is `this`, of that signature.

#### @spec a-body-of-several-formulas-is-said-as-them-holding-together

> The verbalizer says a block of formulas on lines of their own, as a body or as a formula, as the formulas holding together.

This follows because Alloy reads the formulas of a block as joined by `and`.

#### @spec an-empty-body-is-said-as-what-the-definition-names

> The verbalizer says a definition with an empty body as what it names, for every parameter.

This follows because an empty body always holds, so the predicate holds for every value of each parameter.

#### @spec a-formula-that-always-holds-is-left-out-of-an-and

> The verbalizer leaves a formula that always holds out of an `and`. An empty block is one, and so is a call of a predicate with an empty body.

This follows because `a and true` claims what `a` claims.

#### @spec a-formula-that-only-always-holds-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a formula that always holds and is not part of an `and`, and says that it claims nothing.

This follows because no words of the readings say a formula that claims nothing, and a statement that said nothing would hide that.

#### @spec a-parameter-that-can-hold-several-things-or-none-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a definition with a parameter declared with `lone`, `some` or `set`, or with an arrow, and names the parameter.

Derives from: [`spec-a-variable-that-can-hold-several-things-or-none-is-refused`](#spec-a-variable-that-can-hold-several-things-or-none-is-refused)

This follows because the definition says "for every" value of each parameter, and the readings have no words for every set of things.

#### @spec a-function-is-said-as-its-value-holding-a-member-exactly-when-its-body-does

> The verbalizer says `fun f[x: T]: U { e }` as: for every `x` and every member `u` of `U`, the reading of `f` of `x` and `u` "exactly when" `u in e`.

This follows because a function names its value, and its value holds a member exactly when the body does.

#### @spec a-call-of-a-function-with-a-reading-is-said-with-its-reading

> The verbalizer says `y in f[x]`, for a function `f` with a reading, with the reading of `f`, with `x` and then `y` in its slots.

This follows because the reading says when the value of `f` holds a member, which is what `y in f[x]` claims.

#### @spec a-call-of-a-function-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body

> The verbalizer says a call of a function with no reading by its body, with each argument in the place of its parameter.

Derives from: [`spec-a-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body`](#spec-a-predicate-with-no-reading-is-said-by-its-body)

This follows because the value of a call is the body with the arguments in place.

#### @spec a-call-of-a-macro-is-said-by-its-body

> The verbalizer says a call of a macro, `let m[x] = …` or `let m[x] { … }`, by its body with each argument in the place of its parameter.

This follows because Alloy puts a macro's body in the place of each call, with an argument for each parameter.

#### @spec a-macro-as-a-definition-is-refused

> The verbalizer refuses a macro given as a definition, and says that a parameter of a macro has no type.

Derives from: [`spec-a-parameter-with-no-type-is-refused`](#spec-a-parameter-with-no-type-is-refused)

This follows because the verbalizer says a definition "for every" value of each parameter, and a parameter with no type has no noun.

#### @spec a-definition-says-what-it-names-exactly-when-its-body-holds-for-every-parameter

> The verbalizer says a [definition](#term-definition-passage) as "for every" parameter, then the name, "exactly when", and the body.

This follows because a definition fixes the meaning of a word for every value, and "exactly when" says that it holds in both directions.

#### @spec a-definition-that-marks-its-variables-disj-is-said-with-them-different

> The verbalizer says a definition that marks its variables `disj` with the condition that they are different. A call of it said by its body gets the same condition.

This follows because `disj` before the variables of a predicate adds that condition to its body.

#### @spec a-definition-with-a-body-of-one-clause-is-said-on-one-line

> The verbalizer says a definition whose body is one clause on one line after the "for every".

This follows because a short definition is clearest as one sentence.

#### @spec a-definition-whose-body-is-a-series-sets-it-apart

> The verbalizer sets apart the body of a [definition](#term-definition-passage) that is a series, below "exactly when the following holds".

This follows because a series after "exactly when" could end before its last clause and leave that clause outside the definition. "x is quiet exactly when x has run, and at the next moment, x has stopped" reads two ways. The verbalizer sets apart a side of a rule that holds a series for the same reason. The sweep found three such definitions once its reading back took in definitions too.

#### @spec a-definition-says-each-parameter-with-the-noun-of-its-type

> The verbalizer says each parameter of a definition with the noun of its type.

This follows because each parameter is a thing, and the noun tells which kind.

#### @spec a-definition-is-said-in-markdown-the-way-a-formula-is

> In the Markdown layout, the verbalizer says a definition with a blank line between its paragraphs.

This follows because the statement sits in a Markdown document, and a definition in it reads as paragraphs like any other statement.

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-for-each-kind

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-for-each-kind:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When all of these hold:
> - the alternatives of a [definition](#term-definition-passage) each begin with the kind of the subject
> - the definition can be said [kind by kind](#term-by-kind)
>

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-for-each-kind:end -->

A definition by cases reads best as a short list with one noun phrase per kind, such as "a spec that cites no axiom". A reader takes that in faster than a sentence about a unit that is a spec. The verbalizer writes it this way when each alternative begins with its kind and the verbalizer can say the definition kind by kind.

```alloy
all f: Definition | (f in GuardedByKind and byKind[f]) implies f in PhrasePerKind
```

#### @spec the-alternatives-of-one-kind-are-put-together-with-or

<!-- statement-spec-the-alternatives-of-one-kind-are-put-together-with-or:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [definition](#term-definition-passage) has two alternatives for one kind and can be said [kind by kind](#term-by-kind), [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as one noun phrase for that kind, with the alternatives joined by or.
<!-- statement-spec-the-alternatives-of-one-kind-are-put-together-with-or:end -->

When the verbalizer says a definition kind by kind, two alternatives for the same kind are just two ways to be that kind. So they share one noun phrase for the kind, joined by "or".

```alloy

```

#### @spec the-options-of-an-or-inside-a-kind-are-one-coordination

<!-- statement-spec-the-options-of-an-or-inside-a-kind-are-one-coordination:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [definition](#term-definition-passage) has an or inside one kind and can be said [kind by kind](#term-by-kind), [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as one run of clauses joined by commas and or.
<!-- statement-spec-the-options-of-an-or-inside-a-kind-are-one-coordination:end -->

In a definition that the verbalizer can say kind by kind, one kind can offer a choice through an "or". The verbalizer then says its options as one flat run, like "names, names or is", joined by commas and "or". A flat run reads at once, where nested choices would not.

```alloy
all f: Definition | (f in OrInsideKind and byKind[f]) implies f in OneCoordination
```

#### @spec a-definition-with-one-kind-is-one-sentence

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-with-one-kind-is-one-sentence:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When the alternatives of a [definition](#term-definition-passage) are of one kind and the definition can be said [kind by kind](#term-by-kind), [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as one sentence.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-with-one-kind-is-one-sentence:end -->

A list of one line is no list. So when the verbalizer can say a definition kind by kind but all its alternatives share one kind, it says the definition as one sentence.

```alloy
all f: Definition | (f in OneKind and byKind[f]) implies f in OneSentenceKind
```

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-does-not-begin-with-its-kind

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-does-not-begin-with-its-kind:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [definition](#term-definition-passage) has an alternative that does not begin with its kind, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as a list of the alternatives as they stand.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-does-not-begin-with-its-kind:end -->

A phrase for a kind has to start with the kind. Forced into that shape, an alternative that opens with something else would lose part of what it says. So when any alternative does not begin with its kind, the verbalizer lists the alternatives as they stand.

```alloy

```

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-a-run-of-and-would-read-two-ways

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-a-run-of-and-would-read-two-ways:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [definition](#term-definition-passage) has a run of "and" beside another alternative of its kind, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as a list of the alternatives as they stand.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-a-run-of-and-would-read-two-ways:end -->

Merged into one phrase for their kind, a run of "and" next to another alternative of that kind could join to the wrong one. The reader should not have to guess which. So when a definition has such a run, the verbalizer lists the alternatives as they stand.

```alloy
all f: Definition | f in AmbiguousAnd implies f in AsItStands
```

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-is-not-about-its-subject

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-is-not-about-its-subject:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [definition](#term-definition-passage) has an alternative that says something about another unit, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as a list of the alternatives as they stand.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-an-alternative-is-not-about-its-subject:end -->

A phrase for a kind describes the subject. An alternative that says something about another unit would come out as if it were about the subject. So when a definition has such an alternative, the verbalizer lists the alternatives as they stand.

```alloy
all f: Definition | f in NotAboutSubject implies f in AsItStands
```

#### @spec a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-two-of-its-kinds-can-share-a-member

<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-two-of-its-kinds-can-share-a-member:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [definition](#term-definition-passage) has two kinds that can share a member, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the definition as a list of the alternatives as they stand.
<!-- statement-spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-it-stands-when-two-of-its-kinds-can-share-a-member:end -->

A definition said kind by kind reads "is one of these", and a reader can take that as exactly one. Where the kinds share no member, as signatures that extend one signature do, nothing is of two kinds, and both readings say the same. Where two kinds can share a member, a thing of both kinds that meets both alternatives would seem left out. So the verbalizer lists the alternatives as they stand, below "at least one of these holds".

```alloy
all f: Definition | f in KindsShareAMember implies f in AsItStands
```

#### @spec a-word-that-names-a-term-links-to-the-unit-that-holds-its-reading-in-markdown

> In the Markdown layout, the verbalizer links a word whose reading a unit holds to that unit.

This follows because a reader who meets the word can follow it to what it means.

#### @spec a-word-that-names-a-term-is-plain-in-the-text-layout

> In the text layout, the verbalizer says a word whose reading a unit holds in plain words.

This follows because the text layout has no way to hold a link.

#### @spec only-the-first-mention-of-a-term-links

> In a [linked formula](#term-linked-formula), the verbalizer links only the first mention of a term, in reading order.

This follows because a link on every mention fills the page with blue, and the reader learns the term once.

#### @spec a-word-never-links-to-the-unit-its-sentence-is-in

> The verbalizer never links a word to the unit whose statement it is saying.

This follows because a link to the page the reader is on goes nowhere.

#### @spec a-reading-that-points-at-a-unit-links-to-it

> The verbalizer links a word whose reading points at a unit to that unit.

This follows because the author wrote the link by hand to name exactly where the word leads.

#### @spec a-link-in-a-table-held-in-another-document-goes-through-its-path

> The verbalizer writes a link of a table held in another document, to an anchor of that document, through the path to it.

This follows because a link written as `#anchor` points into the document that holds the table, and a reader meets the words in another.

#### @spec the-nouns-of-a-quantifier-link-and-the-article-follows-the-word

> The verbalizer links the noun of a quantified type whose reading a unit holds, and chooses the article by the word, not the bracket.

This follows because the variable is a thing of the type, so a reader may follow the noun. A bracket must not change a or an.

#### @spec a-sentence-starts-with-a-capital-on-the-word-and-not-on-the-bracket

> When a statement begins with a linked word, the verbalizer puts the capital on the first letter of the word, inside the link.

This follows because the capital belongs to the first letter a reader sees.

#### @spec a-reading-held-by-no-unit-has-plain-words

> The verbalizer says a word whose reading no unit holds in plain words, even in the Markdown layout.

This follows because a word with no unit to lead to is only a word.

#### @spec a-variable-said-once-takes-the-place-of-its-quantifier-as-a-noun-phrase

<!-- statement-spec-a-variable-said-once-takes-the-place-of-its-quantifier-as-a-noun-phrase:end -->

#### @spec a-quantifier-whose-variable-would-be-said-twice-is-said-in-full

<!-- statement-spec-a-quantifier-whose-variable-would-be-said-twice-is-said-in-full:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->

<!-- statement-spec-a-quantifier-with-a-time-phrase-in-one-of-several-conditions-is-said-in-full:end -->


<!-- statement-spec-a-condition-that-is-not-about-the-variable-is-said-in-full:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->

```alloy

```

#### @spec three-clauses-or-fewer-are-said-in-a-sentence

<!-- statement-spec-three-clauses-or-fewer-are-said-in-a-sentence:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->

#### @spec a-longer-list-or-a-list-with-a-comma-is-bullets

<!-- statement-spec-a-longer-list-or-a-list-with-a-comma-is-bullets:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [list](#term-series) is a run of clauses joined by and or by or and cannot be put in a [sentence](#term-sentenceable), [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list as bullets.
<!-- statement-spec-a-longer-list-or-a-list-with-a-comma-is-bullets:end -->

A sentence loses the reader when it carries many conditions, commas inside items, or items longer than a clause. Bullets give each item its own line. So any run of "and" or "or" that cannot go in a sentence goes in bullets.

```alloy
all f: Series | (f in Items and not sentenceable[f]) implies f in AsBullets
```

##### @spec a-list-of-more-than-three-clauses-is-bullets

<!-- statement-spec-a-list-of-more-than-three-clauses-is-bullets:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [list](#term-series) has more than three clauses, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list as bullets.
<!-- statement-spec-a-list-of-more-than-three-clauses-is-bullets:end -->

Four conditions in one sentence lose the reader. So a list of more than three clauses is always bullets.

```alloy
all f: Series | f in Many implies f in AsBullets
```

##### @spec a-list-with-a-comma-in-an-item-and-more-than-two-clauses-is-bullets

<!-- statement-spec-a-list-with-a-comma-in-an-item-and-more-than-two-clauses-is-bullets:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When all of these hold:
> - a [list](#term-series) has an item that holds a comma
> - the list has more than two clauses
>
> then [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list as bullets.
<!-- statement-spec-a-list-with-a-comma-in-an-item-and-more-than-two-clauses-is-bullets:end -->

A comma inside an item makes a list of three read as a list of more. So once a list has such a comma and more than two clauses, it is bullets.

```alloy
all f: Series | (f in CommaItem and f in MoreThanTwo) implies f in AsBullets
```

##### @spec a-list-too-long-for-a-line-is-bullets

<!-- statement-spec-a-list-too-long-for-a-line-is-bullets:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [list](#term-series) is longer than a line when it is put in a sentence, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list as bullets.
<!-- statement-spec-a-list-too-long-for-a-line-is-bullets:end -->

A sentence that runs past a line is hard to take in at once. So a list that would make such a sentence is bullets, no matter how few its clauses.

```alloy
all f: Series | f in TooLong implies f in AsBullets
```

##### @spec a-list-with-a-time-phrase-before-its-last-clause-is-bullets

<!-- statement-spec-a-list-with-a-time-phrase-before-its-last-clause-is-bullets:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [list](#term-series) has a clause before its last that begins with a time phrase, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list as bullets.
<!-- statement-spec-a-list-with-a-time-phrase-before-its-last-clause-is-bullets:end -->

A time phrase early in a sentence seems to cover every clause after it. In the formula it covers only its own clause. So a list with a time phrase before its last clause is bullets, where each clause stands alone.

```alloy
all f: Series | f in TimeBeforeLast implies f in AsBullets
```

##### @spec a-list-with-a-relative-clause-before-its-last-clause-is-bullets

<!-- statement-spec-a-list-with-a-relative-clause-before-its-last-clause-is-bullets:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [list](#term-series) has a clause before its last with a relative clause in it, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list as bullets.
<!-- statement-spec-a-list-with-a-relative-clause-before-its-last-clause-is-bullets:end -->

In running prose a relative clause has no visible end, so it seems to swallow the clauses after it. "An owner that pulse has disposed and code has registered c" reads as one long description of the owner. In the formula, the relative clause ends with its own item. So when a clause before the last has a relative clause, the [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) puts the list in bullets. The line break then marks where that clause stops.

```alloy
all f: Series | f in RelativeBeforeLast implies f in AsBullets
```

##### @spec a-list-with-a-clause-that-holds-its-own-and-or-or-is-bullets

> The verbalizer says a list as bullets when a clause in it has two names for a subject: "o and p are the same".

This follows because the "and" of that subject reads like the "and" of the list. In "c has run, o and p are the same and d has run", a reader cannot tell where each clause ends.

##### @spec an-item-that-is-more-than-a-clause-makes-the-list-bullets

<!-- statement-spec-an-item-that-is-more-than-a-clause-makes-the-list-bullets:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [list](#term-series) has an item that is more than one clause, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list as bullets.
<!-- statement-spec-an-item-that-is-more-than-a-clause-makes-the-list-bullets:end -->

A sentence can carry a list only while each item is a single clause. An item that is more than one clause, such as one with its own quantifier or its own list, would blur into its neighbours. So one such item is enough: the [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the whole list as bullets.

```alloy
all f: Series | f in NotClause implies f in AsBullets
```

#### @spec negative-clauses-that-share-their-words-are-said-once-before-none-of-these

<!-- statement-spec-negative-clauses-that-share-their-words-are-said-once-before-none-of-these:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When all of these hold:
> - a [list](#term-series) is a run of negative clauses about one subject that share their verb, each before a noun phrase of its own
