Some lists hold only negative clauses about one subject, and every clause goes on from the same verb with a noun phrase of its own. There the verbalizer says the subject and the verb once, with "none of these" after them. The bullets then hold only the noun phrases: "the definition has none of these:", then "an alternative that does not begin with its kind". It cuts the shared words before the first word of a noun phrase, so they hold no noun phrase.

```alloy

```

#### @spec an-and-inside-an-or-is-kept-apart

<!-- statement-spec-an-and-inside-an-or-is-kept-apart:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> For every [list_1](#term-series):
>

<!-- statement-spec-an-and-inside-an-or-is-kept-apart:end -->

Read aloud, "a and b or c" has two meanings, and a statement must have one. So when one alternative in a list holds an "and", the [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) sets the list out as bullets. Their grouping leaves only one reading.

```alloy
all f: Series | f in AndInOr implies f in KeepsAndApart
```

#### @spec words-said-once-for-several-clauses-hold-no-noun-phrase

> Where the verbalizer says once the words that several clauses share, those words hold no noun phrase. They are the subject, and at most the verb after it.

This follows because a noun phrase covers the noun phrases after it in its clause. Said once, "is a definition with" would put "a definition" ahead of every phrase below it. It would then say that the thing is a definition, which no clause on its own said.

Each form that says shared words once stops before the first noun phrase. That holds for [a subject said once](#spec-a-subject-is-said-once-when-clauses-begin-with-it) and for the "is not" of [several negations](#spec-several-negations-of-a-variable-are-one-negation). It holds for the "is" before [the kinds of a definition](#spec-a-definition-by-cases-is-said-as-a-noun-phrase-for-each-kind), and for the verb before ["none of these"](#spec-negative-clauses-that-share-their-words-are-said-once-before-none-of-these).

#### @spec a-subject-is-said-once-when-clauses-begin-with-it

> In a list said as a sentence, the verbalizer says once a subject that its clauses begin with.

This follows because "unit_1 is a spec and sits in no unit" says it once, and repeating it adds nothing.

#### @spec a-pair-of-variables-is-said-as-it-is-and-not-as-a-subject

> In a list said as a sentence, the verbalizer says a clause about a pair of variables as it is, not as a shared subject.

This follows because "unit_1 and unit_2 are different" is about both, and cannot be the subject of another clause.

#### @spec a-rule-keeps-its-then-before-a-time-phrase

<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-keeps-its-then-before-a-time-phrase:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When all of these hold:
> - a [list](#term-series) is a rule whose two sides are each one clause
> - the list is not a rule whose first side begins with a time phrase
> - the list is a rule whose second side begins with a time phrase
>
> then [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list with "then" before the time phrase.
<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-keeps-its-then-before-a-time-phrase:end -->

A short rule can stumble on a time phrase. Without "then", it puts two commas in a row: "when this, now or later, that". With it, the rule reads cleanly. So the [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) keeps the "then" when both sides are single clauses and only the second opens with a time phrase.

```alloy
all f: Series | (f in OneLineRule and f not in TimeFirst and f in TimeSecond) implies f in KeepsThen
```

#### @spec a-rule-drops-its-then-before-anything-else

<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-drops-its-then-before-anything-else:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When all of these hold:
> - a [list](#term-series) is a rule whose two sides are each one clause
> - the list is not a rule whose first side begins with a time phrase
> - the list is not a rule whose second side begins with a time phrase
>
> then [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list without "then".
<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-drops-its-then-before-anything-else:end -->

When both sides of a rule are single clauses, the comma in "when this, that" already shows where the second side starts. A "then" after every "when" would add words and nothing else. So the [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) leaves it out, unless a time phrase opens either side.

```alloy
all f: Series | (f in OneLineRule and f not in TimeFirst and f not in TimeSecond) implies f in DropsThen
```

#### @spec a-rule-whose-first-side-begins-with-a-time-phrase-puts-its-then-on-a-line-of-its-own

<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-whose-first-side-begins-with-a-time-phrase-puts-its-then-on-a-line-of-its-own:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [list](#term-series) is a rule whose first side begins with a time phrase, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list with "then" at the start of the second side, on a line of its own.
<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-whose-first-side-begins-with-a-time-phrase-puts-its-then-on-a-line-of-its-own:end -->

A time phrase at the head of a rule might seem to cover the second side too. On one line the reader would have to guess. So the second side starts on a line of its own with "then", which shows where the time phrase stops.

```alloy
all f: Series | f in TimeFirst implies f in ThenOwnLine
```

#### @spec a-rule-with-a-list-for-a-side-puts-its-then-on-a-line-of-its-own

<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-with-a-list-for-a-side-puts-its-then-on-a-line-of-its-own:begin — generated by `canon generate`; edits are overwritten -->
> When a [list](#term-series) is a rule with a first side and a second and is not a rule whose two sides are each one clause, [verbalizer](#term-verbalizer) says the list with "then" at the start of the second side, on a line of its own.
<!-- statement-spec-a-rule-with-a-list-for-a-side-puts-its-then-on-a-line-of-its-own:end -->

A rule with a side longer than one clause cannot fit on a line. So its second side starts on a line of its own, and "then" tells the reader where it begins.

```alloy

```

#### @spec a-rule-that-is-a-side-of-a-rule-is-set-apart

> The verbalizer sets a rule that is a side of another rule apart, below "the following holds".

This follows because a "when" inside a "when", or an "otherwise" after two of them, would not show which rule each part belongs to.

#### @spec a-first-side-that-holds-a-time-phrase-is-set-apart

> The verbalizer sets the first side of a rule apart, below "when the following holds", when the side holds a time phrase.

This follows because a reader could take the time phrase as covering the second side too, even when "then" starts a line of its own.

#### @spec a-side-that-holds-a-comma-is-set-apart-where-no-then-marks-the-second-side

> When a rule would stand on one line with no "then", the verbalizer sets apart a side with a comma of its own. When both sides hold one, it sets the second side apart.

This follows because the comma would read as where the second side starts. On one line, "then" stands only before a time phrase. In "when r, a, and at the next moment, b", a reader could put "a" in the first side.

#### @spec a-condition-that-is-a-series-is-said-as-a-list

> The verbalizer sets apart a condition that is a series of clauses, "a, b and c", as a list with one clause to a line.

This follows because the comma of a series in a condition would read as the end of the condition. A list ends where its last item does, and puts each clause on a line of its own.

#### @spec a-comma-of-a-reading-after-then-is-left-on-its-line

> The verbalizer leaves on its line a second side whose only comma is inside the words of a reading, such as ", such as …" or ", with …".

This follows because a comma inside a reading is the author's and ends with the reading. A reader cannot take it as the end of the condition, which ended at the comma before. A reading's comma in the first side is still set apart.

#### @spec a-second-side-that-holds-a-time-phrase-before-an-otherwise-is-set-apart

> In a rule with an "otherwise", the verbalizer sets the second side apart when it holds a time phrase, the one it begins with included.

This follows because a reader could take the time phrase as covering the "otherwise" too.

#### @spec a-second-or-last-side-of-a-rule-that-holds-a-series-is-set-apart

> The verbalizer sets apart a side of a rule after "then" or "otherwise" when that side is a series of clauses after a comma.

This follows because a reader could take the last clause of the series as a claim of its own, outside the rule. An example is "a, and at the next moment, b".

## @axiom a-short-list-of-rules-settles-what-english-leaves-open

> A short list of rules settles what English leaves open, so that each statement means only what its formula means.

English leaves some things open that a formula fixes: where a phrase stops, which noun a "that" follows, and from when "now" counts. The verbalizer settles each of these one way, and the rules below say which. A reader learns them once. A probe can then ask whether readers really read that way. Attempto Controlled English keeps such rules for the same reason.

#### @spec a-noun-phrase-covers-the-clause-it-stands-in

> A noun phrase says its quantifier over the clause it stands in, and over nothing beyond it. "The cleanup is on no owner" says that no owner has the cleanup on it.

This follows because the clause is the smallest stretch of words that holds the noun phrase. A reader looks no further for what it covers.

#### @spec the-first-noun-phrase-of-a-clause-covers-the-next

> Of two noun phrases in one clause, the first covers the second. "No cleanup is on an owner" says that no cleanup is on any owner.

This follows because a reader meets the first phrase first, and takes what follows as said of what it names.

#### @spec a-relative-clause-says-more-of-the-noun-it-follows

> A relative clause, "that …", says what else holds of the noun right before it. An "and" inside it joins only its own conditions.

This follows because "that" points back to the nearest noun. The verbalizer puts a relative clause only where nothing follows that its "and" could take in.

#### @spec the-noun-alone-names-the-one-thing-of-its-kind

> "The cleanup" names the one cleanup the statement speaks of. Where two things of one kind are in play, each keeps its number, as "cleanup_1" and "cleanup_2" do.

This follows because "the" picks out one thing, and a reader can tell which one only when one thing of that kind is in play.

#### @spec now-is-the-moment-a-statement-is-read-at

> "Now" is the moment a reader takes the statement at. Inside "from now on" or "at the next moment", it is each moment that phrase picks.

This follows because a time phrase moves the reader to the moments it names, and the words below it hold there.

#### @spec a-time-phrase-covers-the-rest-of-its-sentence

> A time phrase covers the words after it up to the end of its sentence. Where it ends in a colon, it covers the lines set apart below it.

This follows because a reader has no other mark of where a time phrase stops. So the verbalizer sets apart below it any words with a time phrase of their own.

#### @spec until-then-stops-before-its-moment

> "b now or later, and until then, a" says that b holds at some moment from now on. It says that a holds at every moment from now up to that one, and maybe not at it.

This follows because "until then" ends where "then" starts, as "I wait until five" does. Any moment of b gives the same truth, so the words need not say the first. On timelines built to catch each misreading, five of five readers took it this way.

#### @spec the-bullets-below-a-colon-are-the-parts-of-its-line

> The bullets below a line that ends in a colon are the parts of what that line says. Their indentation shows which line they belong to.

This follows because a list ends where its last item does, so no part of it can read as more of another.

#### @spec a-sentence-joins-its-clauses-with-and-or-with-or-never-both

> A sentence joins its clauses with "and" or with "or", and never with both. A list shows how such clauses group.

This follows because "a and b or c" groups two ways, and a reader cannot tell which one the formula holds.

#### @spec exactly-when-goes-both-ways-and-when-goes-one

> "x exactly when y" says that each holds where the other does. "When x, y" says that y holds wherever x does, and nothing of the moments without x.

This follows because a reader takes "when" as a rule and "exactly when" as both ways. "The light is on exactly when the switch is down" reads so.

#### @spec another-differs-from-the-thing-of-its-kind-named-last

> "Another unit" and "no other unit" differ from the unit the words named last before them. That unit is in the same clause, in the clause before it, or where a quantifier introduced it.

This follows because a reader looks back for what "other" points at, as for "the". A subject that a series leaves out is not in the words, so it is not what a reader finds.

#### @spec one-of-these-names-one-of-kinds-that-share-no-member

> "x is one of these:" says that x is what one of the phrases below it names. The phrases name kinds that share no member, so x is never two of them.

This follows because "one of these" leaves open whether x may be more than one of them. Kinds that share no member settle it: "one" and "at least one" then say the same, so a reader is right either way.

#### @spec a-noun-the-words-name-again-in-a-when-is-every-thing-of-its-kind

> "A bug" stands for every bug where "the bug" follows it, in the first side of a rule or as the subject of "exactly when". "When a bug has run, code has registered the bug" says that of each bug.

This follows because in English, "a" in a "when" speaks of whichever thing meets the condition. "The bug" after it points back at that thing, so the rule holds of each bug.

#### @spec each-statement-reads-back-to-its-meaning

> Read by these rules, the words of each statement have one meaning, and it is the meaning of what the verbalizer said.

This follows because the rules are only of use if they settle each statement one way. A parser reads the words of the sweep back by the rules, the words of its definitions too. It finds one reading for each statement, and that reading means what the printed IR means.

#### @spec each-fixed-word-of-the-printer-reads-back-to-its-meaning

> Each fixed word of the printer stands in a statement that reads back to its one meaning. These are the intros of its lists, its time phrases, the parts of `until` and `since`, and the words of rules and of comparisons.

This follows because the sweep reads back only what its formulas happen to reach. The parser reads a fixed word that no statement holds by a rule that nothing checks. Each fixed word has a statement of its own here, so the test reads back a word the printer gains from the start.
